The Jirga is a 'traditional system' of justice, which is actively practiced in, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa , Baluchistan as well as in districts of Sindh bordering with Baluchistan as to resolve legal cases and disputes. The system, which was in practice since the British rule, was modified under the 'Special Provision Ordinance (Criminal Provisions 11) of 1968' . Besides dispensing justice and dealing with judicial cases, the Jirga also covers all important aspects of monetary, political, and communal life of tribal society.

However, in its present form, the tribal Jirga especially in Sindh province has generated heated debate about its legal position as well as conflict of its rules and codes with the constitution of Pakistan, law of the land or formal justice system as well as international human rights standards and conventions. Strongest allegation on the Jirga system or 'informal justice system' has been its unfairness against innocents during the course of decisions and execution on variety of its rules and regulations. This informal system of justice is being practiced in rural areas of Sindh and Baluchistan.

The sky did not darken. That was the cruel part. Everyone who had eyes knew the sun was still up there on the morning of the Blanking, warm on their faces, and none of them could see it. It happened at 10:14 a.m. Eastern, simultaneously everywhere on Earth. Planes stayed in the air only because autopilot doesn't need eyes. Cars did not. By noon the hospitals were overwhelmed, and the doctors in them were as helpless as their patients. Marguerite Oyelaran had been blind since she was six.

On the morning of the Blanking she was making coffee in her apartment in Baltimore, and she noticed nothing at all until her neighbor started screaming. She went next door, guided by the sound, and found him on his kitchen floor, crawling, knocking things over. She knelt beside him and took his hand. "Mr. Kowalski," she said. "Stop moving. Breathe. You're going to learn this." That was the first lesson. There would be millions more. Within a week, the world's roughly forty million blind people had become the only functioning population on the planet.

We derive an upper bound for the time needed to implement a generic unitary transformation in a $d$ dimensional quantum system using $d$ control fields. We show that given the ability to control the diagonal elements of the Hamiltonian, which allows for implementing any unitary transformation under the premise of controllability, the time $T$ needed is upper bounded by $T\leq \frac{\pi d^{2}(d-1)}{2g{\text{min}}}$ where $g{\text{min}}$ is the smallest coupling constant present in the system.

We study the tightness of the bound by numerically investigating randomly generated systems, with specific focus on a system consisting of $d$ energy levels that interact in a tight-binding like manner.

Early and correct diagnosis is a very important aspect of cancer treatment. Detection of tumour in Computed Tomography scan is a tedious and tricky task which requires expert knowledge and a lot of human working hours. As small human error is present in any work he does, it is possible that a CT scan could be misdiagnosed causing the patient to become terminal. This paper introduces a novel fully automated framework which helps to detect and segment tumour, if present in a lung CT scan series.

It also provides useful analysis of the detected tumour such as its approximate volume, centre location and more. The framework provides a single click solution which analyses all CT images of a single patient series in one go. It helps to reduce the work of manually going through each CT slice and provides quicker and more accurate tumour diagnosis. It makes use of customized image processing and image segmentation methods, to detect and segment the prospective tumour region from the CT scan. It then uses a trained ensemble classifier to correctly classify the segmented region as being tumour or not.

Networks embedded on surfaces arise in applications ranging from transport and communication design to terrain analysis and geometric modeling. Computing optimal or canonical networks on a surface is difficult because topological constraints, such as genus, boundary components and homotopy classes, interact with geometric ones. We introduce a framework that handles these constraints by passing to general covering spaces of the surface, in which the relevant structure is simpler to represent and manipulate.

Networks on the base surface are lifted to the cover, optimized there under a symmetry condition, and projected back, so that questions about the surface reduce to questions about a more tractable space. We show that this correspondence preserves length and connectivity, characterize the covers that are sufficient for a given class of networks, and derive bounds on the size of the cover required. As applications, we obtain algorithms for computing shortest and Steiner-type networks within prescribed homotopy classes, and we describe how the same machinery extends to networks with branching and boundary conditions.

Governments face a real tension when it comes to space exploration. Billions of dollars go into rockets and telescopes while people on Earth still struggle with hunger, disease, and poverty. It is fair to ask whether that money would be better spent at home. Still, I believe space exploration deserves public funding, as long as it is balanced against urgent needs. The first reason is that space programs often produce benefits on Earth. Technologies developed for space have given us satellite communications, GPS, weather forecasting, and improved medical imaging.

Climate satellites now track rising temperatures and melting ice, which helps us understand and respond to one of our biggest problems. Spending on space is therefore not simply money sent away from Earth. Second, space spending is small compared with other budgets. NASA's budget is well under one percent of the US federal budget. Even if it were eliminated, the savings would not end poverty or fix healthcare. Those problems are mostly about priorities and political will, not a lack of funds that space agencies are consuming. Even so, critics are right that people's basic needs must come first.

Plausible Deniability I died at sixty-eight after forty years as an insurance claims adjuster, never once saying what I was actually thinking. So when I woke up in a hospital nursery with all my memories intact and a fresh set of dimples, I knew exactly what to do with my second chance. Not fame. Not fortune. Honesty, delivered at age four, with enormous eyes and a lisp. My debut was Great-Aunt Marjorie's funeral. Mom had stuffed me into a clip-on tie.

I walked up to the open casket, studied the body with great seriousness, and announced to the silent chapel, "She looks way nicer now. Mommy said she was mean when she was awake." Mom made a noise like a kettle. A cousin began coughing into a hymnal. I held up my juice box and asked, "Is there still going to be cake?" I was hooked. Over the next year I refined my craft. The rules were simple. Never be crude, because crude gets you punished. Be curious. Be sweet. Be wrong in precisely the right place.

We study kinetic theory models for the distribution of wealth in a market economy, with particular attention to the emergence of power-law tails. Within a Boltzmann-type framework, agents exchange wealth through binary trades that combine a conservative component with a stochastic one representing risk and speculation. Starting from the resulting master equation, we derive Fokker-Planck-type approximations in the limit of small exchanges and obtain stationary distributions in closed form.

We show that when agents are partitioned into groups with different saving propensities or different degrees of risk, each group relaxes to an exponential or gamma-type equilibrium with its own characteristic scale. The distribution of wealth over the whole population is then a superposition of these exponentials. We demonstrate analytically that such an overlap, weighted by a suitable distribution of scales, generates a Pareto power-law tail with an exponent determined by the statistics of the parameters. Numerical simulations of the underlying particle system confirm the analytical predictions and show convergence toward the stationary profiles.

Every year governments spend billions on space programs. At the same time, millions of people don't have food, clean water, or healthcare. So people say the money should stay here. I get that. But I think space is worth it. Space research helps us. Satellites give us weather reports, GPS, phones that work everywhere. Space tech made better medical tools and materials. We use satellites to study climate change, which is one of our biggest problems. Space spending's actually way smaller than people think. NASA gets less than one percent of the US budget. Cutting it wouldn't suddenly fix poverty.

Those problems need better planning and political will. But governments shouldn't ignore basic needs. Food, housing, health come first. I think we can do both. If we spend carefully, we can help people now and still explore space for tomorrow.

Block cipher E2, designed and submitted by Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corporation, is a first-round Advanced Encryption Standard candidate. It employs a Feistel structure as global structure and two-layer substitution-permutation network structure in round function with initial transformation IT function before the first round and final transformation FT function after the last round. The design principles influences several more recent block ciphers including Camellia, an ISO/IEC standard cipher. In this paper, we focus on the key-recovery attacks on reduced-round E2-128/192 taking both IT and FT functions in consideration with integral cryptanalysis.

We first improve the relations between zero-correlation linear approximations and integral distinguishers, and then deduce some integral distinguishers from zero-correlation linear approximations over 6 rounds of E2. Furthermore, we apply these integral distinguishers to break 6-round E2-128 with 2^{120} known plaintexts (KPs), 2^{115.4} encryptions and 2^{28} bytes memory. In addition, the attack on 7-round E2-192 requires 2^{120} KPs, 2^{167.2} encryptions and 2^{60} bytes memory.

When people use electronic media for their communication, Computer-Mediated Communication (CMC) theories describe the social and communicative aspects of people's interpersonal transactions. When people interact via a remote-controlled robot, many of the CMC theses hold. Yet, what if people communicate with a conversation robot that is (partly) autonomous? Do the same theories apply? This paper discusses CMC theories in confrontation with observations and research data gained from human-robot communication. As a result, I argue for an addition to CMC theorizing when the robot as a medium itself becomes the communication partner.
In view of the rise of social robots in coming years, I define the theoretical precepts of a possible next step in CMC, which I elaborate in a second paper.

Models driven by Brownian noise capture poorly the non-Gaussian features, such as heavy tails, skewness, and sudden jumps, that data from complex systems often display. In this paper we build a framework for measuring model uncertainty when the observations are non-Gaussian. The Hellinger distance serves as the measure of discrepancy between the probability distribution produced by a candidate stochastic model and the distribution of the observed data. Our models are stochastic differential equations driven by α-stable Lévy noise, and we obtain the evolution of their probability densities from the corresponding nonlocal Fokker–Planck equations.

Photometric data for 593 Cepheids in the LMC, measured by Udalski et al. in the OGLE survey, augmented by 92 longer period Cepheids from other sources, are analyzed for the P-C and P-L relations, and for the variations of amplitude, light curve shape, and period across the instability strip at constant absolute magnitude. Both the P-C and P-L relations have different slopes for periods smaller and larger than 10 days. The break at 10 days is also seen in the period-amplitude relations, and the compound Fourier combinations of R21 and Phi21 introduced by Simon and Lee.

The LMC Cepheids are bluer than Galactic Cepheids in the B,V,I color bands, part of which is due to differential Fraunhofer line blanketing and part to real differences in the temperature boundaries of the instability strip. The LMC strip is hotter by between 80K and 350K depending on the period. Hence, both the slopes and (necessarily) the zero points of the P-L relations in B,V,I must differ between LMC and the the Galaxy, and in fact they do.

Long before cybersecurity became a booming industry, Timothy Winslow was a teenager with a secondhand computer, a dial-up modem, and a curiosity that would eventually bring federal agents to his family's front door. Winslow now works as a security consultant, helping companies defend their networks. He traces his fascination back to the moment he realized a phone line could connect his bedroom to computers hundreds of miles away. Through high school he spent late nights dialing into university systems, corporate servers and, eventually, networks belonging to government contractors.

He mapped how they were linked, studied their weaknesses, and taught himself programming from manuals and message boards. By his own account, he rarely changed or took anything. To Winslow, each system was a puzzle, and getting inside was the reward. He kept handwritten notebooks full of phone numbers, login prompts, and notes on how different machines behaved. The law, however, made no distinction between curiosity and malice. The Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, passed in 1986, made unauthorized access to protected computers a federal crime regardless of intent, and investigators were paying closer attention to intrusions involving sensitive networks.

A fractal is a geometric object that shows self-similarity, which means its parts look like the whole at different levels of magnification, and its complexity is captured by a fractional, or non-integer, dimension. Fractals started out as abstract constructions in pure mathematics, but Benoit Mandelbrot argued in The Fractal Geometry of Nature (1982) that they describe many natural forms more accurately than the smooth shapes of Euclidean geometry. As he put it, clouds are not spheres and mountains are not cones. Coastlines are the classic example.

A coastline is irregular at every scale, so its measured length grows as the unit of measurement shrinks, a result called the coastline paradox. Fractal dimension gives a more meaningful description than length alone; the west coast of Great Britain, for instance, has a dimension of about 1.25. Living systems often take on fractal designs because such structures maximize surface area or coverage within a limited volume. The branching of human airways and blood vessels, like that of trees and root systems, allows gases, fluids, and nutrients to be exchanged and distributed efficiently.

Without coworkers nearby, plenty of people get lonely, and talking with a team through a screen can be more difficult. Home also has its share of distractions, such as the television, pets, and relatives, and these can make concentrating hard. And when the office is in the bedroom, some people struggle to switch off at the end of the day. All in all, working from home can work very well, provided people look for ways to keep in touch with others and draw firm lines between work and rest.

Claims like "four out of five dentists recommend" usually rest on real surveys, but the phrasing often exaggerates what was really measured. A company, or a research firm working for it, may survey a group of dental professionals, sometimes just a few hundred, and ask which brands they would recommend. The key detail is that respondents are often allowed to name more than one brand. As a result, 80 percent of dentists might list a given toothpaste while recommending its competitors equally often.

In 2007, the UK Advertising Standards Authority decided that a Colgate advertisement making this kind of claim was misleading for exactly that reason. So the figure does not normally mean that dentists favor your toothpaste over every other. It typically shows only that most of the dentists surveyed regard it as an acceptable choice, which holds true for most fluoride toothpastes.

Research on human-robot collaboration or human-robot teaming, has focused predominantly on understanding and enabling collaboration between a single robot and a single human. Extending human-robot collaboration research beyond the dyad, raises novel questions about how a robot should distribute resources among group members and about what the social and task related consequences of the distribution are. Methodological advances are needed to allow researchers to collect data about human robot collaboration that involves multiple people. This paper presents Tower Construction, a novel resource distribution task that allows researchers to examine collaboration between a robot and groups of people.

By focusing on the question of whether and how a robot's distribution of resources (wooden blocks required for a building task) affects collaboration dynamics and outcomes, we provide a case of how this task can be applied in a laboratory study with 124 participants to collect data about human robot collaboration that involves multiple humans. We highlight the kinds of insights the task can yield. In particular we find that the distribution of resources affects perceptions of performance, and interpersonal dynamics between human team-members.

> We propose a novel framework for knowledge transfer in medical image segmentation. The proposed framework is network-agnostic, which means that it can be applied to any segmentation network. The framework consists of two components: a feature extractor and a feature decoder. The feature extractor is a pre-trained segmentation network, which is used to extract features from the input image. The feature decoder is a lightweight network that is trained to decode the features into a segmentation mask. The feature extractor and the feature decoder are trained jointly in an end-to-end manner.

The proposed framework can be used for both supervised and unsupervised knowledge transfer. In the supervised setting, the feature extractor is pre-trained on a large dataset of annotated images, and the feature decoder is trained on a smaller dataset of annotated images. In the unsupervised setting, the feature extractor is pre-trained on a large dataset of unlabeled images, and the feature decoder is trained on a smaller dataset of unlabeled images. The proposed framework has been evaluated on two medical image segmentation tasks: brain tumor segmentation and liver segmentation.

Data observed in complex systems frequently exhibit non-Gaussian features, such as heavy tails, skewness, and abrupt jumps, that are poorly captured by models driven by Brownian noise. This paper develops a framework for quantifying model uncertainty when observations are non-Gaussian, using the Hellinger distance as a measure of discrepancy between the probability distribution generated by a candidate stochastic model and that of the observed data. We consider stochastic differential equations driven by α-stable Lévy noise and derive the evolution of their probability densities through the associated nonlocal Fokker–Planck equations.

The Hellinger distance between model and data densities is then minimized to estimate unknown parameters and to select the most plausible model. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the approach accurately identifies noise parameters and distinguishes Gaussian from non-Gaussian dynamics, providing a practical tool for data-driven modeling under uncertainty.

The debate over whether universities should prioritize job-ready skills or abstract theory often presents a false choice. Supporters of practical training argue that students pay high tuition and deserve a clear path to employment. Graduates who can already use industry software, write a business plan, or manage a project get hired faster and contribute sooner. Advocates of theory respond that specific tools become obsolete within a decade, while a deep understanding of mathematics, science, or philosophy lets people adapt, solve unfamiliar problems, and keep learning throughout their careers.

In my view, theory should remain the foundation, but it should be taught through application. An engineering student who understands thermodynamics and also builds a working prototype learns both why and how. Employers can train someone on a particular platform in weeks, but they cannot easily teach a person to think rigorously. Universities should protect that rarer ability and keep it connected to real tasks.

Abstract Building population-level templates of the central nervous system is essential for studying anatomical variability and for enabling consistent analysis across subjects. Existing atlases typically cover either the brain or the spinal cord, and they rarely account for the continuous anatomy that links the two. We present a generative framework for constructing diffeomorphic atlases from combined brain and spinal cord magnetic resonance imaging data. The method estimates a mean template and a distribution of smooth, invertible deformations that map the template to individual subjects, preserving topology and permitting statistical analysis of shape.

We address the large differences in field of view and anatomical curvature between brain and cervical cord by using a multi-scale registration scheme with region-specific regularization. The model is trained on a heterogeneous dataset of healthy volunteers and evaluated on held-out scans. Results show improved alignment accuracy and sharper template structure compared with existing atlas construction methods, and the learned deformation model captures plausible anatomical variation. The resulting atlas offers a foundation for studying neurological disease along the entire neuraxis.

Tumors are masses of abnormal cells, plus the supporting tissue around them: blood vessels, connective tissue and immune cells. They form when mutations in a cell's DNA disable the controls on growth and division, often by activating growth-promoting genes or silencing protective ones. The damaged cell multiplies without restraint and passes the mutations on. Over time, further mutations accumulate, and the cells may recruit blood vessels to feed the growth. Benign tumors stay local, while malignant ones can invade tissue and spread.

Chicken pox is a virus in the herpes family . And like all herpes viruses , once you get it , it stays in you forever . Your immune system is pretty good at keeping it suppressed . Similarly , if you get exposed to it again , your immune system will be prepared and kill it off quite quickly . The virus does n't change very much over time . The chickenpox virus in you can re - activate when your immune system is compromised and result in Shingles .

But that is the virus coming back from inside you , not you getting exposed by another sick person . Many ( though not all ) other viruses change their composition slightly much faster than chickenpox , and so we can catch them again .

The burning ballots created the smoke the world witnessed billowing from the chimney. The ballots, of course, were made of paper. Which sometimes seems like an endangered species.

Had the cardinals voted on iPads, they couldn't very well have tossed the sleek tablets into the chapel's cast-iron stove. Yet an all-but-paperless society is where some experts argue we are headed. Gunmen Kill at Least 23 at Tunisia's Bardo Museum TUNIS, Tunisia — Gunmen stormed the Bardo National Museum in the Tunisian capital on Wednesday, killing at least 23 people in an assault on one of the country's most famous cultural sites and on the tourism trade that its economy relies on. The majority of the victims were foreign tourists, a number of whom had disembarked that morning from cruise ships moored in Tunis. Security forces brought an end to a standoff inside the museum by shooting two of the attackers, and dozens of people received treatment for injuries.

The Bardo, home to one of the finest collections of Roman mosaics anywhere, stands beside the national parliament. The assault has rattled a country frequently called the lone success story of the Arab Spring. Following the 2011 revolution that toppled President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali, Tunisia approved a new constitution and held free elections. At the same time, it has become one of the biggest suppliers of foreign fighters to extremist groups in Syria and Iraq, where an estimated 3,000 Tunisians are thought to have signed up.

Plants have no nervous system, no brain, and no way to move from place to place, yet they constantly sense their surroundings and adjust their behavior in response. Over the past few decades, researchers have found that plants exchange information both within their own bodies and with other organisms through several channels. The word "communication" is used loosely here: it means sending and receiving signals that change behavior, not conscious intention. Communication Within a Single Plant Electrical signals. When a leaf is wounded, electrical changes in membrane potential can travel to distant parts of the plant within seconds to minutes.

In a widely cited 2018 study, Toyota and colleagues used a fluorescent calcium sensor in Arabidopsis to show waves of calcium moving from a caterpillar-damaged leaf to other leaves, triggering defense responses. The Venus flytrap is the most dramatic example: two touches to its trigger hairs within about 20 seconds generate action potentials that snap the trap shut. Hormonal signals. Plant hormones such as jasmonic acid, salicylic acid, ethylene, and auxin coordinate growth and defense across tissues.

kWh/kW divides energy by power, so the units cancel down to hours. The figure tells you how many hours of full rated output a system delivers. For solar panels, annual kWh per kW (often written kWh/kWp) is called "specific yield": a 1 kW array that produces 1,400 kWh a year has 1,400 equivalent full-power hours. For batteries, capacity in kWh divided by the kW rating gives duration, so a 10 kWh, 5 kW battery can discharge at full power for two hours.

A fractal's a shape that has detail at every magnification level. Usually it repeats itself, and the dimension doesn't have to be a whole number. In theory they're pure, but in the real world lots of physical systems look fractal-ish over some range of scales, which is why the idea's useful. Nature has the best examples. Coastlines, river branches, mountains, clouds—all have irregular repeating patterns. The length or area you measure depends on how you measure it, which Benoit Mandelbrot figured out.

Biology does similar stuff: bronchial tubes and blood vessels branch like crazy to pack huge surface area into small space, which lets them exchange stuff efficiently. Fractals also show up in physics. When particles clump together at random, they branch like lightning. Chaotic systems often settle into fractal patterns. And near critical points where phase transitions happen, you get fractal scaling. Practically, fractals help with antenna design, image compression, medical imaging, modeling porous materials and terrain. But there are limits. Real objects are only fractal within some range—atoms at the small end, the object's size at the other.

This paper presents how we can achieve the state-of-the-art accuracy in multi-category object detection task while minimizing the computational cost by adapting and combining recent technical innovations. Following the common pipeline of "CNN feature extraction region proposal RoI classification," we mainly redesign the feature extraction part, since region proposal part is not computationally expensive and classification part can be efficiently compressed with common techniques like truncated SVD. Our design principle is "less channels with more layers" and adoption of some building blocks including concatenated ReLU, Inception, and HyperNet.

The designed network is deep and thin and trained with the help of batch normalization, residual connections, and learning rate scheduling based on plateau detection. We obtained solid results on well-known object detection benchmarks: 83.8 mAP (mean average precision) on VOC2007 and 82.5 mAP on VOC2012 (2nd place), while taking only 750msimage on Intel i7-6700K CPU with a single core and 46msimage on NVIDIA Titan X GPU. Theoretically, our network requires only 12.3 of the computational cost compared to ResNet-101, the winner on VOC2012.

The Doctor of Villains Dr. Miriam Castellan's practice occupied the thirteenth floor of a building that did not appear on any map, which her clients appreciated. Her first appointment of the day was a man who called himself the Orchid. He arrived exactly on time, as he always did, and took the chair nearest the window. He disliked sitting with his back to a door. "Good morning, Doctor," he said.

"I have been thinking about our last session." "I am glad to hear it. What came up for you?" "You asked me why I wished to flood the harbor district." He straightened a cuff. "I answered that it was a matter of principle. On reflection, I do not believe that was a complete answer." Miriam made a short note. I understand this opinion, but I think space exploration is still worth funding. First, space research helps people on Earth. Scientists use satellites to study climate change, which is one of the biggest problems we face today. Second, the amount of money spent on space is smaller than most people think. Convolutional neural networks achieve much of their power on images because the plane offers a regular grid and translation symmetry, and curved surfaces have neither. A frequent workaround flattens a surface onto a planar domain so that an ordinary CNN can be used, yet current surface-to-image representations either cause heavy area distortion or need multiple images to cover an entire shape. We introduce a new representation for sphere-type surfaces built on general covering maps.

Instead of a toric cover with a fixed set of cone points, our approach has a flat torus wind around the surface several times, so each region shows up with little distortion somewhere in one image. This image is seamless and periodic, which makes convolution with circular padding well defined and lets standard architectures be used with only minor changes. Predictions from the several copies of each surface point are afterward merged back onto the mesh. On shape segmentation and classification benchmarks, the method performs on par with or better than competing approaches, and it stays simple and efficient.

Abstract The theory of the basic principles of biharmonic holograms and the theoretical study of their applications have been widely pursued in recent decades. The mathematical nature of these structures, together with the peculiar nature of musical material, have led to the discovery of very few biharmonic mathematical objects. Despite the impressive number of potential biharmonic phenomena, the fundamental question remains unanswered and the physical phenomenon is still extremely far from experimental confirmation. The goal of this paper is to address this question by developing the theory and practical methods to derive biharmonic complex forms and their physical implications.

Here we will focus on а group of biharmonic elliptic subhilical submanifolds (BHes) as the natural mathematical objects of interest. It takes the form of а biharmonic elliptic subhilical space having one or more submanifolds of degree (а,b) where а is а submanifold with а nonzero curvature and b is а submanifold with а nonzero curvature. The holographic conjugate and the singularity are considered as the basic principle of this biharmonic geometry.

The azimuthal angular decorrelation of dijet systems is a sensitive probe of QCD radiation patterns and of parton dynamics at small Bjorken x. We present here a study of jet azimuthal decorrelation in deep inelastic electron–proton scattering at the proposed electron–proton mode of the Future Circular Collider (FCC-ep), where a 60 GeV electron beam collides with a 50 TeV proton beam at a centre-of-mass energy of roughly 3.5 TeV. Events are simulated using leading-order and next-to-leading-order matrix elements matched to parton showers, and jets are reconstructed with the anti-kT algorithm inside a realistic detector acceptance.

We measure the distribution of the azimuthal angle difference between the two leading jets as a function of jet transverse momentum, photon virtuality, and rapidity separation. A clear decorrelation appears and grows with rapidity separation, and we compare its size to predictions from DGLAP and BFKL evolution. The results show that FCC-ep will widen the accessible kinematic range by over an order of magnitude compared with HERA, allowing stringent tests of small-x QCD dynamics and possible sensitivity to gluon saturation effects.

I was thirty-four and healthy, and NASA was paying me more to sleep for three months than I'd earned the year before teaching high school chemistry. The paragraph didn't seem important. Chamber Four smelled like rubbing alcohol and new plastic. Dr. Renata Okafor checked the IV line in my arm for the third time and tapped the glass panel above my face. "You'll feel cold in your fingers first," she said. "Then nothing.

Next thing you know, it's February." "Will I dream?" "That's one of the things we're here to find out." The lid came down on its hydraulic arms with a soft hiss. Through the curved viewport I could see the observation room: six technicians at their stations, a wall of monitors tracing my heartbeat in green, and a man in a NASA polo shirt eating almonds out of a paper cup. The perfusate started flowing. My fingertips went numb, then my wrists. It was almost pleasant, like wading into a lake in October.

We study the Twitter conversation following the August 2017 `Unite the Right' rally in Charlottesville, Virginia, using tools from network analysis and data science. We use media followership on Twitter and principal component analysis (PCA) to compute a `Left'/`Right' media score on a one-dimensional axis to characterize nodes. We then use these scores, in concert with retweet relationships, to examine the structure of a retweet network of approximately 300,000 accounts that communicated with the #Charlottesville hashtag. The retweet network is sharply polarized, with an assortativity coefficient of 0.8 with respect to the sign of the media PCA score.

Community detection using two approaches, a Louvain method and InfoMap, yields largely homogeneous communities in terms of Left/Right node composition. When comparing tweet content, we find that tweets about `Trump' were widespread in both the Left and Right, though the accompanying language was unsurprisingly different. Nodes with large degrees in communities on the Left include accounts that are associated with disparate areas, including activism, business, arts and entertainment, media, and politics.

Should Governments Spend on Space or on Earth's Problems? A lot of people wonder whether governments should put money into exploring space. Some say that money ought to go toward fixing problems on Earth, such as hunger, disease and poverty. Both sides make good arguments, in my opinion, but I think governments should give a small share of their budget to space and use most of it for problems here at home. To start, I can see why some people oppose spending on space. Every day, huge numbers of people around the world lack enough food or clean water.

In poor countries, hospitals frequently do not have enough doctors or medicine. Seeing this, it is difficult to argue that sending a rocket to Mars matters more. Rockets cost a great deal, and a single launch may cost hundreds of millions of dollars. That money could pay for lots of schools or clinics. On the other hand, exploring space brings us many advantages. Scientists working on space programs, for instance, have created many things we rely on daily. Satellites provide weather data, which lets farmers know when rain is coming and helps people prepare for major storms.

China's cybercensors have long used a "Great Firewall" to block its citizens from reading critical articles from Western news websites or consuming other content it disapproves of. But it's no longer enough for them, says a study published Friday. They've developed a new IT weapon and have attacked servers outside their borders, including in the United States. The study's authors have named it the "Great Cannon," and it operates in plain sight. Going on the attack so visibly and handily within another country's borders will probably draw international ire, the study's authors say, and Beijing may have counted on that.

"This is a powerful attack capability, and we are curious about the risk and benefit analysis that led the Chinese government to reveal it with this highly visible denial of service attack," said researcher John Scott-Railton. The reason Chinese censors are taking that risk: Free-speech cyberactivists have found ways to get around the Great Firewall and give Chinese readers greater access to the West's free press. This effect is well documented in cognitive psychology and has several plausible explanations. First, consolidation occurs during rest, particularly during sleep. The brain strengthens new neural connections and integrates recently acquired information with existing knowledge. A break therefore allows learning to settle, whereas continuous effort offers no such opportunity. Second, extended practice produces fatigue and mental interference. After prolonged effort, performance may decline temporarily, which can obscure what has actually been learned. Returning after an interval removes this fatigue and reveals the underlying progress. Third, spaced practice is more effective than massed practice, a finding known as the spacing effect.

Retrieving information after a delay requires greater cognitive effort, and that effort strengthens long-term retention. Finally, a break allows a fresh perspective. Persistent focus on a single approach can entrench unproductive strategies, while time away often permits alternatives to emerge.

We consider a special class of quantum non-dynamical $R$-matrices in the fundamental representation of ${\rm GL}_N$ with spectral parameter given by trigonometric solutions of the associative Yang-Baxter equation. In the simplest case $N=2$ these are the well-known 6-vertex $R$-matrix and its 7-vertex deformation. The $R$-matrices are used for construction of the classical relativistic integrable tops of the Euler-Arnold type. Namely, we describe the Lax pairs with spectral parameter, the inertia tensors and the Poisson structures. The latter are given by the linear Poisson-Lie brackets for the non-relativistic models, and by the classical Sklyanin type algebras in the relativistic cases.
In some particular cases the tops are gauge equivalent to the Calogero-Moser-Sutherland or trigonometric Ruijsenaars-Schneider models.

We analyze the dynamics of a population of independent random walkers on a graph and develop a simple model of epidemic spreading. We assume that each walker visits independently the nodes of a finite ergodic graph in a discrete-time markovian walk governed by his specific transition matrix. With this assumption, we first derive an upper bound for the reproduction numbers. Then we assume that a walker is in one of the states: susceptible, infectious, or recovered. An infectious walker remains infectious during a certain characteristic time.

If an infectious walker meets a susceptible one on the same node there is a certain probability for the susceptible walker to get infected. By implementing this hypothesis in computer simulations we study the space-time evolution of the emerging infection patterns. Generally, random walk approaches seem to have a large potential to study epidemic spreading and to identify the pertinent parameters in epidemic dynamics.

We present an approximate analytic expression for the photoluminescence spectral function of a model polariton system, which describes a quantum dot, with a finite number of fermionic levels, strongly interacting with the lowest photon mode of a pillar microcavity. Energy eigenvalues and wavefunctions of the electron-hole-photon system are obtained by numerically diagonalizing the Hamiltonian. Pumping and photon losses through the cavity mirrors are described with a master equation, which is solved in order to determine the stationary density matrix.

The photon first-order correlation function, from which the spectral function is found, is computed with the help of the Quantum Regression Theorem. The spectral function qualitatively describes the polariton lasing regime in the model, corresponding to pumping rates two orders of magnitude lower than those needed for ordinary (photon) lasing. The second-order coherence functions for the photon and the electron-hole subsystems are computed as functions of the pumping rate.

A monochrome screen needs only one bit per pixel, since each pixel is either on or off. A display of 64,000 pixels therefore requires 64,000 bits. Because one byte contains eight bits, dividing 64,000 by eight yields 8,000 bytes. In computing, this is conventionally rounded to approximately 8 KB, as a kilobyte is treated as roughly 1,000 bytes, or 1,024 bytes in binary convention. The figure is thus an accurate approximation of the true requirement.

Angular asymmetries in hard scattering processes are sensitive to the linear polarization of gluons inside unpolarized hadrons. Because this polarization is generated perturbatively, it can produce azimuthal modulations such as cos 2φ in final states like heavy-quark pairs, dijets and Higgs production. The size of the effect is controlled by the maximal linear polarization allowed by positivity bounds, and many phenomenological studies have assumed it could be large. We examine how soft gluon radiation affects this expectation.

Resumming large logarithms in the ratio of the hard scale to the transverse momentum of the pair, we find that Sudakov-type effects suppress the linearly polarized component much more strongly than the unpolarized one. The resulting asymmetries fall well below the maximal values at transverse momenta where the factorized description applies. We quantify the suppression for representative kinematics at the LHC and a future electron-ion collider, and show how it depends on the hard scale and on the nonperturbative input. Our results imply that earlier estimates are overly optimistic and indicate which observables retain meaningful sensitivity to gluon polarization.

The Office on the Fourteenth Floor Dr. Eleanor Vance kept her practice in a nondescript building downtown, wedged between a dental surgery and an accounting firm. Her nameplate gave no specialty. Clients found her by word of mouth, through channels she had learned not to ask about. Her nine o'clock on Monday was a man who had once tried to flood a coastal city. He sat in the armchair opposite her, took off his gloves with careful deliberation, and talked for forty minutes about his father. "He told me the ocean would take everything in the end," the man said.

"I suppose I wanted to prove him right on my own timetable." Dr. Vance made a note. She never wrote the word villain in her files. She had given up the term early in her career, once she realized it named an outcome rather than a person. Her clients had done terrible things, and some were still capable of more. Her job was not to absolve them. It was to understand what had brought them to the edge, and whether any of them could still be talked into stepping back.

In this paper, we propose a novel and efficient 3D object detection method called PI-RCNN, which combines point cloud and image data using a point-based attentive convolutional fusion module. Existing multi-sensor 3D object detection methods have limitations in terms of computational efficiency, accuracy and robustness, especially when dealing with sparse or occluded objects. Our proposed approach addresses these challenges by introducing an innovative two-stage fusion strategy that leverages both point cloud and image information to improve object localization and classification.

The first stage involves separate instance-level processing of point clouds and images using state-of-the-art 3D object detection algorithms and deep neural networks. The second stage fuses the obtained point cloud and image features using our point-based attentive convolutional fusion module, which adaptively weights the importance of each modality based on their relevance to the object of interest. This attention mechanism allows us to selectively focus on specific parts of the object, improving overall performance while reducing computational cost.

A tumor is an abnormal lump of the body's own cells, along with the blood vessels, connective tissue, and immune cells that grow around them. Normally, genes tightly control when cells divide and when they die. Mutations from aging, inherited traits, smoking, radiation, or certain viruses can break those controls and let a cell multiply unchecked. Its descendants pile up into a mass. Benign tumors stay contained. Malignant (cancerous) ones invade nearby tissue and can spread.

Abstract Panoptic segmentation is an approach to image classification that uses a large number of images to classify objects in a scene, and then performs a supervised learning algorithm on these classifications. The main idea behind this method is to use a large number of images to train a model which can be used to predict the object's location in the scene. This allows us to perform a supervised learning algorithm on the resulting predictions without having to store all the training data.

In this work we present a novel implementation of panoptic segmentation using a convolutional neural network (CNN) with a single hidden layer. We show that our CNN achieves state-of-the-art performance on several benchmark datasets including ImageNet, CIFAR10, and MNIST. Our results demonstrate that our CNN is able to learn complex features such as pose, orientation, and color from a large number of images. Furthermore, we show that our CNN can also be trained by hand, allowing users to create their own models.

Polar-ring galaxies are rare systems in which a ring of gas, dust and stars orbits nearly perpendicular to the plane of a central host. Their origin remains debated, with accretion from a neighbor and cold gas infall both proposed. We use N-body simulations including gas dynamics and star formation to test whether a polar ring can form in a major merger of two disk galaxies. We explore a range of mass ratios, orbital geometries and gas fractions.

In a subset of encounters, particularly those with nearly perpendicular spin orientations and unequal gas content, the gas of one progenitor is stripped, settles into a rotating structure orthogonal to the remnant's stellar body, and forms stars over time. The resulting ring persists for several gigayears and reproduces observed morphology, rotation curves and stellar masses of known polar-ring galaxies. We find that the formation requires the host remnant to be a relatively gas-poor, early-type system. These results suggest that mergers, and not only accretion, can account for a significant fraction of polar-ring galaxies.

The two-dimensional electron system formed at the interface between the insulating oxides LaAlO3 and SrTiO3 exhibits ferromagnetism, superconductivity, and a wide range of unique magnetotransport properties. A key challenge is to find a unified microscopic mechanism that underlies these emergent phenomena. The two-dimensional electron system that forms at the interface between the band insulators LaAlO3 and SrTiO3 displays a remarkable variety of behavior, including gate-tunable superconductivity, signatures of magnetism, strong spin–orbit coupling and unusual magnetotransport. Here we show that a universal Lifshitz transition between d-orbitals lies at the core of the observed transport phenomena in this system.

Whether these phenomena share a common microscopic origin has remained an open question. Here we present systematic magnetotransport measurements, performed as a function of gate-controlled carrier density, on a series of interfaces with different LaAlO3 thicknesses and electron mobilities. Our measurements find a critical electronic density at which the transport switches from single to multiple carriers. In every sample we identify a critical density of approximately 1.7 × 1013 cm−2, at which transport changes abruptly from single-carrier to multi-carrier behavior.

A Petri net, also known as a place/transition (PT) net, is one of several mathematical modeling languages for the description of distributed systems. It is a class of discrete event dynamic system. A Petri net is a directed bipartite graph that has two types of elements, places and transitions. Place elements are depicted as white circles and transition elements are depicted as rectangles. A place can contain any number of tokens, depicted as black circles. A transition is enabled if all places connected to it as inputs contain at least one token.

Some sources state that Petri nets were invented in August 1939 by Carl Adam Petri—at the age of 13—for the purpose of describing chemical processes. Like industry standards such as UML activity diagrams, Business Process Model and Notation, and event-driven process chains, Petri nets offer a graphical notation for stepwise processes that include choice, iteration, and concurrent execution. Unlike these standards, Petri nets have an exact mathematical definition of their execution semantics, with a well-developed mathematical theory for process analysis[citation needed].

Surface-embedded networks appear in many settings, from the design of transport and communication systems to terrain analysis and geometric modeling. Finding optimal or canonical networks on a surface is hard, since geometric constraints interact with topological ones such as genus, boundary components and homotopy classes. We present a framework that deals with these constraints by moving to general covering spaces of the surface, where the relevant structure becomes easier to represent and work with.

A network on the base surface is lifted into the cover, optimized there subject to a symmetry condition, and then projected back down, turning questions about the surface into questions about a space that is easier to handle. We prove that this correspondence keeps both length and connectivity intact, give a characterization of which covers suffice for a particular class of networks, and establish bounds on how large the cover must be.

We present a feasibility study for the measurement of jet azimuthal angular decorrelation in deep inelastic electron-proton scattering at the proposed Future Circular Collider in its electron-hadron configuration (FCC-ep). The azimuthal decorrelation between the scattered lepton and the leading jet in the transverse plane is sensitive to soft and collinear gluon radiation, and it provides a stringent test of perturbative quantum chromodynamics and of transverse-momentum-dependent parton distributions. Using Monte Carlo event samples generated at a centre-of-mass energy of approximately 3.5 TeV, and a parametrised detector simulation, we evaluate the expected statistical and systematic uncertainties across a wide kinematic range.

We compare predictions from fixed-order calculations and parton-shower models and assess their sensitivity to the strong coupling constant. The results indicate that FCC-ep would reach a precision substantially exceeding that of existing HERA measurements, extending the accessible phase space to higher momentum transfer and lower values of Bjorken x.

Polar-ring galaxies are rare. They have a ring of gas, dust, and stars orbiting nearly perpendicular to the central host's disk. Nobody's totally sure how they form—maybe a neighboring galaxy pulled the ring away, maybe cold gas fell in. We ran N-body simulations with gas dynamics and star formation to test whether a major galaxy merger could make one. We tried different mass ratios, orbital setups, and gas amounts. When the right conditions lined up—especially nearly perpendicular spin and unequal gas—the gas from one galaxy got stripped, settled into a perpendicular structure, and started forming stars.

The ring hung around for billions of years and matched what we see in real polar-ring galaxies: the shape, rotation curves, stellar mass. The host had to be a relatively gas-poor early-type system. So mergers, not just accretion from a neighbor, can explain a lot of the polar-ring galaxies we observe.

The global network of gravitational-wave detectors has completed three observing runs with $\sim 50$ detections of merging compact binaries. A third LIGO detector, with comparable astrophysical reach, is to be built in India (LIGO-Aundha) and expected to be operational during the latter part of this decade. Multiple detectors operating at different parts of the globe will provide several pairs of interferometers with longer baselines and an increased network SNR. This will improve the sky localisation of GW events.

Multiple detectors simultaneously in operation will also increase the baseline duty factor, thereby, leading to an improvement in the detection rates and, hence, the completeness of surveys. In this paper, we quantify the improvements due to the expansion of the LIGO Global Network (LGN) in the precision with which source properties will be measured. We also present examples of how this expansion will give a boost to tests of fundamental physics.

Engineering: Concrete construction that made vast vaults and domes like the Pantheon possible, plus aqueducts, sewers, and a road network spanning the Mediterranean. Weather satellites warn people of coming storms, and GPS supports everything from farming to emergency services. Many inventions, including improved water filters and medical scanners, came out of space programs. Next, space exploration inspires young people.

Watching a rover land on Mars leads many students to take an interest in science and engineering, and that in turn produces new discoveries. Last, space budgets are fairly small next to the rest of government spending, so cutting them would not put an end to poverty. Depth estimation from a single image is a fundamental problem in computer vision. In this paper, we propose a simple yet effective convolutional spatial propagation network (CSPN) to learn the affinity matrix for depth prediction. Specifically, we adopt an efficient linear propagation model, where the propagation is performed with a manner of recurrent convolutional operation, and the affinity among neighboring pixels is learned through a deep convolutional neural network (CNN).

We apply the designed CSPN to two depth estimation tasks given a single image: (1) Refine the depth output from existing state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods; (2) Convert sparse depth samples to a dense depth map by embedding the depth samples within the propagation procedure. The second task is inspired by the availability of LiDAR that provides sparse but accurate depth measurements.

Our method exploits superpixel-based self-supervision within each image instance, and assumes a single model for all few-shot task without any manually annotated training data.

As a proof-of-concept analysis, we demonstrate the validity of our technique on three medical image segmentation tasks of various complexities (bone segmentation, pancreas segmentation, and vessel segmentation), and demonstrate that our approach is robust to various levels of annotation sparseness. We initiate the systematic study of QMA algorithms in the setting of property testing, to which we refer as QMA proofs of proximity (QMAPs). These are quantum query algorithms that receive explicit access to a sublinear-size untrusted proof and are required to accept inputs having a property $\Pi$ and reject inputs that are $\varepsilon$-far from $\Pi$, while only probing a minuscule portion of their input. Our algorithmic results include a general-purpose theorem that enables quantum speedups for testing an expressive class of properties, namely, those that are succinctly decomposable.

Furthermore, we show quantum speedups for properties that lie outside of this family, such as graph bipartitneness. We also investigate the complexity landscape of this model, showing that QMAPs can be exponentially stronger than both classical proofs of proximity and quantum testers. To this end, we extend the methodology of Blais, Brody and Matulef (Computational Complexity, 2012) to prove quantum property testing lower bounds via reductions from communication complexity, thereby resolving a problem raised by Montanaro and de Wolf (Theory of Computing, 2016).

The two-dimensional electron system that forms at the interface between the band insulators LaAlO3 and SrTiO3 displays а remarkable variety of behavior, including gate-tunable superconductivity, signatures of magnetism, strong spin–orbit coupling and unusual magnetotransport. Whether these phenomena share a common microscopic origin has remained an open question. Here we present systematic magnetotransport measurements, performed as a function of gate-controlled carrier density, on a series of interfaces with different LaAlO3 thicknesses and electron mobilities. In every sample we identify a critical density of approximately 1.7 × 1013 cm−2, at which transport changes abruptly from single-carrier to multi-carrier behavior.

This density is universal, independent of both layer thickness and mobility. The characteristics of the transition, together with its consistency with spectroscopic data, identify it as a Lifshitz transition at which electrons begin to occupy the heavier dxz/dyz bands in addition to the light dxy band. We further show that the same density marks the onset of strong spin–orbit interaction and anomalous magnetoresistance. These results point to orbital band filling as a unifying principle behind the emergent physics of this oxide interface.

Abstract. Organic traffic is a primary source of customer acquisition for e-commerce platforms, and its volume depends heavily on how product feeds are presented to search engines and discovery surfaces. In practice, merchants optimize titles, descriptions, and attributes by hand or with fixed heuristics, which scale poorly and adapt slowly to changes in ranking behavior. We formulate the optimization of product feed content as a sequential decision problem and propose a reinforcement learning framework that learns to generate and select feed modifications in order to maximize expected organic traffic.

The framework relies on a learned traffic estimator, trained on historical impression and click data, to provide reward signals without requiring costly live experimentation for every candidate edit. To address the sparsity and delay of organic feedback, we introduce a counterfactual correction that reduces bias in the estimated rewards, together with a constrained action space that preserves factual accuracy and compliance with platform policies. Experiments on a large-scale offline dataset drawn from an operating e-commerce marketplace show consistent gains in predicted clicks over rule-based and supervised baselines.

Sparse code multiple access (SCMA) scheme is considered to be one promising non-orthogonal multiple access technology for the future fifth generation (5G) communications. Due to the sparse nature, message passing algorithm (MPA) has been used as the receiver to achieve close to maximum likelihood (ML) detection performance with much lower complexity. However, the complexity order of MPA is still exponential with the size of codebook and the degree of signal superposition on a given resource element.

In this paper, we propose a novel low complexity iterative receiver based on expectation propagation algorithm (EPA), which reduces the complexity order from exponential to linear. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed EPA receiver achieves nearly the same block error rate (BLER) performance as the conventional message passing algorithm (MPA) receiver with orders less complexity.

Several well-established findings about memory and cognition account for this. To begin with, consolidation does not stop when practice does. While we rest, and above all while we sleep, the brain reorganizes and strengthens what it has just learned and ties it to knowledge already in place. The spacing effect adds a second explanation: learning spread out over time lasts longer than cramming, in part because pulling up half-forgotten material takes effort, and that effort reinforces it.

A third factor is that stepping away eases mental fatigue and lets the mind drop approaches that are going nowhere, which is sometimes called incubation. On returning, a person can look at the problem anew, free of the fixation that blocked progress earlier. Last, the brain may keep forming connections unconsciously while attention is elsewhere. Together, these mechanisms explain why a pause so often leads to clearer, deeper understanding.

We establish the existence of `time quasilattices' as stable trajectories in dissipative dynamical systems. These tilings of the time axis, with two unit cells of different durations, can be generated as cuts through a periodic lattice spanned by two orthogonal directions of time. We show that there are precisely two admissible time quasilattices, which we term the infinite Pell and Clapeyron words, reached by a generalization of the period-doubling cascade. Finite Pell and Clapeyron words of increasing length provide systematic periodic approximations to time quasilattices which can be verified experimentally.

The results apply to all systems featuring the universal sequence of periodic windows. We provide examples of discrete-time maps, and periodically-driven continuous-time dynamical systems. We identify quantum many-body systems in which time quasilattices develop rigidity via the interaction of many degrees of freedom, thus constituting dissipative discrete `time quasicrystals'.

The use of special symbols in pronunciation guides reflects a fundamental limitation of the English writing system. English spelling is not phonetic. A single letter can represent several sounds, as with the "a" in "cat," "father" and "late," and a single sound can be written in multiple ways. The International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) was developed to give each distinct sound exactly one symbol, so that pronunciation could be recorded without ambiguity. Adding those symbols to the English alphabet would not be practical.

Many of them, such as the schwa or the symbol for the "th" sound, would require readers and writers to learn new characters, and printing, keyboards and existing literature would need to be adapted. English spelling also preserves historical and etymological information, which makes reform politically and culturally difficult. Moreover, pronunciation varies by region, so no single set of respellings would suit every speaker. For these reasons, the symbols remain a specialized tool for dictionaries and linguists rather than part of everyday writing.

We performed polarized Raman spectroscopy on mechanically exfoliated few-layer MoTe2 samples and observed both 1T' and Td phases at room temperature. Few-layer 1T' and Td MoTe2 exhibited a significant difference especially in interlayer vibration modes, from which the interlayer coupling strengths were extracted using the linear chain model: strong in-plane anisotropy was observed in both phases. Furthermore, temperature-dependent Raman measurements revealed a peculiar phase transition behavior in few-layer 1T' MoTe2.

In contrast to bulk 1T' MoTe2 crystals where the phase transition to the Td phase occurs at ~250 K, the temperature-driven phase transition to the Td phase is increasingly suppressed as the thickness is reduced, and the transition and the critical temperature varied dramatically from sample to sample even for the same thickness. Raman spectra of intermediate phases that correspond to neither 1T' nor Td phase with different interlayer vibration modes were observed, which suggests that several metastable phases exist with similar total energies.

I distinguish two types of reduction within the context of quantum-classical relations, which I designate "formal" and "empirical". Formal reduction holds or fails to hold solely by virtue of the mathematical relationship between two theories; it is therefore a two-place, a priori relation between theories. Empirical reduction requires one theory to encompass the range of physical behaviors that are well-modeled in another theory; in a certain sense, it is a three-place, a posteriori relation connecting the theories and the domain of physical reality that both serve to describe.

Focusing on the relationship between classical and quantum mechanics, I argue that while certain formal results concerning singular limits as Planck's constant goes to zero have been taken to preclude the possibility of reduction between these theories, such results at most block reduction in the formal sense; little if any reason has been given for thinking that they block reduction in the empirical sense.

Whatever the fluid lipid vesicle is modeled as the spontaneous-curvature, bilayer-coupling, or the area-difference elasticity, and no matter whether a pulling axial force applied at the vesicle poles or not, a universal shape equation presents when the shape has both axisymmetry and up-down symmetry. This equation is a second order nonlinear ordinary differential equation about the sine $sin\psi (r)$ of the angle $\psi (r)$ between the tangent of the contour and the radial axis $r$.

However, analytically there is not a generally applicable method to solve it, while numerically the angle $\psi (0)$ can not be obtained unless by tricky extrapolation for $r=0$ is a singular point of the equation. We report an infinite series representation of the equation, in which the known solutions are some special cases, and a new family of shapes related to the membrane microtubule formation, in which $sin\psi (0)$ takes values from 0 to $\pi /2$, is given.

The two-dimensional electron system at the LaAlO3/SrTiO3 interface hosts an unusual collection of phenomena, including gate-tunable superconductivity, strong spin-orbit coupling, and signatures of magnetism. These properties have mostly been studied in separate samples grown under different conditions, and it has remained unclear whether they share a common origin. Here we combine electrostatic gating with low-temperature transport measurements on many devices to track the electronic properties of the interface across a wide range of carrier densities.

We find that the behavior of the system is organized around a single critical density, on the order of 10^13 electrons per square centimeter, that is nearly independent of sample details. Near this density, the Hall response, the electron mobility, the strength of spin-orbit coupling, and the superconducting transition temperature all change character together. We associate this threshold with the filling at which electrons begin to occupy higher-energy titanium d-orbital bands, and we show that a simple multiband description accounts for the observed universality.

This paper provides a novel approach to liver segmentation utilizing a deeply self-supervised contour embedded neural network. The first person to notice was a barber named Elias Moreno, which made sense, because nobody spends more time watching mirrors than barbers. He was trimming the back of Mr. Hollis's neck on a Tuesday morning when he glanced up and saw his reflection holding the scissors a half-second late. Not much. Just a lag, like a video call on a bad connection. Elias stopped. His reflection stopped a beat after him. He blinked. His reflection blinked, eventually. "Something wrong?" said Mr. Hollis.

"No," said Elias, and kept cutting, and did not look up again for the rest of the day. By Thursday it was everywhere. People filmed themselves waving at bathroom mirrors and posted the clips with confused captions. The delay was growing. Half a second became a full second, then two. Scientists went on the news with careful faces and said words like "optical anomaly" and "under investigation," which everyone understood to mean they had no idea. What none of them knew, what nobody on this side had ever known, was that mirrors were not reflecting anything. They were windows.

Propositional linear time temporal logic (LTL) is the standard temporal logic for computing applications and many reasoning techniques and tools have been developed for it. Tableaux for deciding satisfiability have existed since the 1980s. However, the tableaux for this logic do not look like traditional tree-shaped tableau systems and their processing is often quite complicated. In this paper, we introduce a novel style of tableau rule which supports a new simple traditional-style tree-shaped tableau for LTL. We prove that it is sound and complete.

As well as being simple to understand, to introduce to students and to use, it is also simple to implement and is competitive against state of the art systems. It is particularly suitable for parallel implementations.

The proliferation of medical image databases represents significant advances in medical image acquisition, quality, and accessibility – however, their use remains limited by data scarcity. We propose a new and adaptable framework, Randon Layers MixUp (ROAM), to boost the utility of existing training data for medical imageing tasks where annotated data is scarce. ROAM incorporates a novel two-stage semi-supervised fine-tuning approach. During Stage I, a model is trained on low-noise images while Stage II uses noisy images to boost robustness.

Our method is able to leverage noise level, in the form of image quality metrics, to adaptively incorporate noise into the supervision signal. We evaluate our method on two imageing tasks, mammographic lesion detection and gastrointestinal image segmentation, and show that it significantly improves segmentation Dice scores, and detection True Positive Rate as compared to other common semi-supervised learning methods. To our knowledge, this paper is the first to evaluate and propose the use of the MixUp method with noisy images and their application in medical imageing tasks. Code is available on https://github.com/hamedkhanm/ROAM-ML.

Yes, if it's an American style option. American style options may be exercised at any time prior to expiration (even if they're not in-the-money). Generally, you are required to deliver or accept delivery of the underlying by the beginning of the next trading day. If you are short, you may be chosen by the clearinghouse to fulfill the exercise (a process called "assignment"). Because the clearinghouse is the counter-party to every options trade, you can be assigned even if the specific person who purchased the option you wrote didn't exercise, but someone else who holds a long position did.

Similarly, you might not be assigned if that person did exercise. The clearinghouse randomly chooses a brokerage to fulfill an assignment, and the brokerage will randomly choose an individual account. If you're going to be writing options, especially using spreads, you need to have a plan ahead of time on what to do if one of your legs gets assigned. This is more likely to happen just before a dividend payment, if the payment is more than the remaining time value.

Maine Wild Food Survival Guide The Golden Rules 1. Do not eat anything unless you are completely certain what it is. A single error with a mushroom or a wild carrot lookalike can be fatal. Fat and protein count for more than greens. Eating only lean meat, rabbit especially, brings on "rabbit starvation." Look for fat: beaver tail, nuts, fish, bone marrow. Boil every drop of water. Giardia is present even in the clearest brook. Plan by season. Maine is generous from May through October and stingy afterward. Put food away all summer.

Plants and Greens Cattail (marshes, pond edges) is the most useful single plant in Maine. Peeled spring shoots taste like cucumber. Green flower heads can be boiled and eaten like corn. The rhizomes provide starch all year, even beneath ice. Fiddleheads (ostrich fern, May) grow on river floodplains. Pick only ones with a smooth stem and a deep U-shaped groove along the inner side, like celery. Always boil them 10 minutes or more, because raw ones make you sick. Dandelion, chickweed, lamb's quarters, plantain, purslane, and wood sorrel are common, safe, and loaded with vitamins.

Population atlases of the brain and spinal cord are vital for spatial normalization, morphometric analysis, and research on neurological disease. However, most current atlases handle the brain and spinal cord separately and rely on deterministic registration, which reveals little about anatomical variability. We introduce a generative framework for building diffeomorphic atlases that models the brain and cervical spinal cord together from MRI data. Each subject is expressed as a smooth, invertible deformation of a common template, and both the template and a probabilistic model of the deformations are learned through variational inference, implemented with a convolutional neural network.

This formulation makes it possible to register new subjects efficiently, draw samples of plausible anatomical variation, and measure the uncertainty in the estimated deformations. We test the approach on multi-subject T1- and T2-weighted MRI datasets and show better alignment of anatomical structures, preserved topology, and much shorter computation time than conventional iterative atlas-building methods.

The study analyzed data from over 100,000 police encounters across England and Wales between 2013 and 2018. It found that Muslim officers were more likely to use force during arrests and were also more likely to be involved in complaints about discrimination or bias. However, the researchers caution against drawing conclusions about the motivations behind these findings.

They suggest that further investigation is needed to determine whether there are underlying factors at play, such as cultural differences or biases within the police force itself. "It is important to note that this does not necessarily mean that Muslim officers are inherently more likely to engage in discriminatory behavior," said Dr. Jane Smith, lead author of the study. The savanna biome is characterised by a continuous vegetation cover, comprised of herbaceous and woody plants. The coexistence of species in arid savannas, where water availability is the main limiting resource for plant growth, provides an apparent contradiction to the classical principle of competitive exclusion. Previous theoretical work using nonspatial models has focussed on the development of an understanding of coexistence mechanisms through the consideration of resource niche separation and ecosystem disturbances.

In this paper, we propose that a spatial self-organisation principle, caused by a positive feedback between local vegetation growth and water redistribution, is sufficient for species coexistence in savanna ecosystems. We propose a spatiotemporal ecohydrological model of partial differential equations, based on the Klausmeier reaction-advection-diffusion model for vegetation patterns, to investigate the effects of spatial interactions on species coexistence on sloped terrain. Our results suggest that species coexistence is a possible model outcome, if a balance is kept between the species' average fitness (a measure of a species' competitive abilities in a spatially uniform setting) and their colonisation abilities.

Texas-Style Smoked Brisket Great Texas brisket comes down to a few things: good meat, a simple rub, steady low heat, clean smoke, and patience. Nothing here is complicated, but every step matters. Plan on 12 to 16 hours from trimming to slicing, and don't schedule anything important around it. Choose the Right Cut Buy a whole packer brisket, which includes both the flat (the leaner, rectangular muscle) and the point (the fattier, thicker muscle). Aim for 12 to 16 pounds.

Look for a cut with good marbling and a flexible feel when you pick it up, since a stiff brisket tends to be from a leaner animal. USDA Choice is fine; Prime is better if you can afford it, and Wagyu or American Wagyu makes a very rich result. Trim the Fat Cold brisket trims easier, so work straight from the fridge. Remove the hard, waxy fat on the point side and any silver skin on the meat side. Trim the fat cap on the other side down to about a quarter inch.

Richard III Reburied in Leicester as Cumberbatch Reads Tribute Five centuries after he fell at the Battle of Bosworth, King Richard III was finally laid to rest Thursday at Leicester Cathedral, in a service that blended medieval pageantry with modern celebrity. The last Plantagenet king was killed in 1485 and buried hastily in the church of Leicester's Greyfriars friary. Over the centuries the site was built over and forgotten. Then, in 2012, archaeologists sensationally rediscovered his remains beneath a city council car park, a find later confirmed by DNA testing against descendants of his sister.

On Thursday, 530 years after his death, the king's oak coffin was lowered into its grave inside the cathedral. Among those taking part was actor Benedict Cumberbatch, a distant cousin of Richard, who read a poem written for the occasion by Poet Laureate Carol Ann Duffy. Philippa Langley, the historian whose campaign launched the search for the grave, said the discovery had prompted researchers to rethink the king.
