The proposal, backed by more than 100 MPs, calls for an elected Senate that would replace the current hereditary system in the Lords. Under this plan, senators would be directly elected by the people, with terms limited to six years. Supporters of the plan argue that it would end the scandal of unelected peers holding significant power over government policy and legislation.

They also say it would ensure that the views of ordinary people are represented in the legislature. However, critics have warned that such a move could lead to a two-chamber parliament dominated by wealthy elites who can afford to campaign extensively for office. They also fear that the loss of tradition and history embodied by the House of Lords could have wider implications for British society. Despite these concerns, supporters of the plan believe that it is necessary if Britain wants to remain a modern, democratic nation.

Consider commuting contractions T and S acting on a Hilbert space H. We call a vector x a joint coboundary when it belongs to the range of both I − T and I − S, and a double coboundary when it belongs to the range of (I − T)(I − S). Any double coboundary is obviously a joint coboundary, so the question we examine is when the reverse is true. In general we prove the inclusion is proper: commuting unitary operators exist, as do commuting contractions coming from measure-preserving actions, whose joint coboundaries are not all double coboundaries.

Conversely, we give sufficient conditions, stated in terms of spectral properties and of whether the relevant ranges are closed, under which the two notions agree. We also discuss applications to the joint behavior of ergodic averages and to solving coupled cohomological equations.

Most of the current face hallucination methods, whether they are shallow learning-based or deep learning-based, all try to learn a relationship model between Low-Resolution (LR) and High-Resolution (HR) spaces with the help of a training set. They mainly focus on modeling image prior through either model-based optimization or discriminative inference learning. However, when the input LR face is tiny, the learned prior knowledge is no longer effective and their performance will drop sharply. To solve this problem, in this paper we propose a general face hallucination method that can integrate model-based optimization and discriminative inference.

In particular, to exploit the model based prior, the Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) denoiser prior is plugged into the super-resolution optimization model with the aid of image-adaptive Laplacian regularization. Additionally, we further develop a high-frequency details compensation method by dividing the face image to facial components and performing face hallucination in a multi-layer neighbor embedding manner. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed method can achieve promising super-resolution results for tiny input LR faces.

It took some time before I realized what I had been handed. It wasn't the knowledge; it was the immunity. Nobody blames a small child for anything. For $N$ spin-polarized fermions with harmonic pair interactions in a $1$-dimensional trap an odd-even effect is found. The spectrum of the $1$-particle reduced density matrix of the system's ground state differs qualitatively for $N$ odd and $N$ even. This effect does only occur for strong attractive and repulsive interactions. Since it does not exists for bosons, it must originate from the repulsive nature implied by the fermionic exchange statistics. In contrast to the spectrum, the $1$-particle density and correlation function for strong attractive interactions do not show any sensitivity on the number parity.
This also suggests that reduced-density-matrix-functional theory has a more subtle $N$-dependency than density functional theory.

Reaching for the Stars Without Neglecting Home Critics have an obvious point to make. Governments pour billions into rockets, probes, and telescopes each year, yet millions of people still have no clean water, medical care, or education, so it seems natural to say the money should be spent here on Earth. But setting space exploration against earthly problems as if they were competitors gets wrong how progress works in both. The argument against space funding hits hard emotionally.

The price of one Mars mission might pay for hospitals or vaccination drives, and with people suffering today, reaching for distant planets can look like an indulgence of rich countries. Still, the budgets are smaller than most people imagine. NASA gets under half a percent of the U.S. federal budget, a sliver next to defense or health spending. Even more significant is that space research pays for itself in practical terms. Satellites follow hurricanes, watch over crops, and record climate change. Water purification, medical imaging, and solar power have all benefited from technology first created for spaceflight.

Product feeds on large e-commerce platforms interleave organic recommendations with sponsored items, and the placement of advertisements has traditionally been optimized for immediate advertising revenue. This short-term focus overlooks a significant side effect: poorly placed or excessive advertisements can depress user engagement with organic content, reducing long-term platform value. In this paper, we formulate advertising allocation in product feeds as a sequential decision-making problem whose objective is to maximize organic traffic while satisfying constraints on advertising exposure and revenue.

We propose a reinforcement learning framework in which an agent determines, at each request, the number and positions of advertisements to insert into a feed, conditioned on user context and the candidate item list. To address the sparsity and delay of engagement signals, we design a reward that combines immediate click feedback with a learned estimate of downstream browsing depth, and we employ a constrained policy optimization scheme to enforce platform-level advertising targets.

In an attempt to combat the increasing danger of cyber threats, a new kind of protection system has been designed - rings of steel. These rings are created to protect vulnerable information and networks by providing several layers of protection that attackers can navigate in order to gain access. The idea of rings of steel is not a new one, but subsequent advances in science have made them more efficient and available to individuals of all styles.

The simple concept is to build a series of circular circles over the information or system being protected, with each circle representing a certain level of protection. The outermost circle is the last line of defence, and it is built to identify and deter potential attacks. This can involve measures such as firewalls, intrusion prevention devices, and security. If an attack is unable to breach this inner layer, they will encounter the first circle, which is designed to slow them down and make it more easy for them to move laterally outside the system.

A new coding scheme for general N-node relay networks is presented for unicast, multicast, and broadcast. The proposed distributed decode-forward scheme combines and generalizes Marton coding for single-hop broadcast channels and the Cover-El Gamal partial decode-forward coding scheme for 3-node relay channels. The key idea of the scheme is to precode all the codewords of the entire network at the source by multicoding over multiple blocks. This encoding step allows these codewords to carry partial information of the messages implicitly without complicated rate splitting and routing. This partial information is then recovered at the relay nodes and forwarded further.

For N-node Gaussian unicast, multicast, and broadcast relay networks, the scheme achieves within 0.5N bits from the cutset bound and thus from the capacity (region), regardless of the network topology, channel gains, or power constraints. Roughly speaking, distributed decode-forward is dual to noisy network coding, which generalized compress-forward to unicast, multicast, and multiple access relay networks.

Adrian Peterson Must Continue Counseling as Part of Suspension, Goodell Says NEW YORK — Minnesota Vikings running back Adrian Peterson will be required to continue counseling and other treatment as a condition of his return to the NFL, Commissioner Roger Goodell said, following Peterson's suspension and guilty plea in a child abuse case. Peterson, who had been suspended by the league, pleaded guilty to misdemeanor reckless assault. The league has said little about the details of the treatment program, including how long it will last or how his progress will be measured. Such conditions are not unusual in NFL disciplinary cases. In artificial intelligence (AI), commonsense reasoning is a human-like ability to make presumptions about the type and essence of ordinary situations humans encounter every day. These assumptions include judgments about the nature of physical objects, taxonomic properties, and peoples' intentions. A device that exhibits commonsense reasoning might be capable of drawing conclusions that are similar to humans' folk psychology (humans' innate ability to reason about people's behavior and intentions) and naive physics (humans' natural understanding of the physical world).

What the Mirror Kept It was meant to be the end of it. A single dose, they promised, and we would never again spend a winter tallying the dead. Six weeks later, the world was empty. The fortunate went peacefully, in their sleep. Everyone else lost their minds, murmuring to people no one else could see, until their bodies quit. Tomas, my husband, passed his final four days in the unlit bathroom, saying sorry to the mirror. By rights I should have gone after him. Same dose, same clinic, same Tuesday.

Yet on the fortieth day I woke up lucid, in an apartment that still carried his smell. Mirrors I stayed away from. I draped a bedsheet over the one in the bathroom and left every other room in darkness. In the empty houses I picked through for supplies, I had come across the mad curled before mirrors, hands pressed flat to the glass, as though they meant to crawl inside. After another week, I had no excuses left. I tugged the sheet down and looked.

It's a bit of both. The Romans freely borrowed from Greece and were well aware of it, as Horace admitted when he wrote that "captive Greece took her savage conqueror captive." Yet they also produced a good deal that was truly their own: Law: A systematic legal tradition, complete with professional jurists and ideas about contracts, property, and the rights of citizens, which still forms the foundation of civil law across Europe and Latin America.

Engineering: Concrete construction, which allowed enormous vaults and domes such as the Pantheon, along with aqueducts, sewers, and a network of roads stretching around the Mediterranean. Governance: Ruling a multiethnic empire for centuries, while step by step giving citizenship to the peoples they had conquered. Literature and art: Verse satire, which Quintilian proudly described as "wholly ours," and a distinctive tradition of portrait busts that were realistic without flinching. Moreover, Greek culture itself owed a great deal to Egypt and the Near East. This is simply how civilizations usually develop: by borrowing and adapting.

> In this work, we propose nnDetection, an end-to-end self-configuring method to detect medical objects in images and videos. Our approach consists of two main components: (1) a novel neural network architecture that can be trained on any dataset with minimal human supervision; and (2) a new loss function that enables our model to learn how to segment and localise objects without requiring bounding box or pixel level labels.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method by training it on 3 different datasets: (i) a synthetic dataset containing 50K images generated using a deep generative model; (ii) a real world dataset consisting of 48K images collected from the internet; and (iii) a large scale clinical dataset comprising over 6M images acquired at multiple hospitals across North America. On all three datasets, our method achieves state-of-the-art performance while being significantly faster than existing methods.

Maine Wild Food Survival Guide First Principles Never eat anything you can't identify with certainty. Learn a few species well rather than many poorly. Boil all water. Beaver ponds and slow streams carry giardia. Calories matter more than vitamins in the first weeks. Fat and starch keep you alive; greens only supplement. Eat nothing raw from animals. Cook thoroughly. Spring (April to June) Fiddleheads (ostrich fern): Tightly coiled, with a smooth stem and a deep U-shaped groove on the inside. Found along river banks. Boil 10 to 15 minutes, discard the water. Never eat them raw.

Wild leeks (ramps): Broad leaves in rich hardwood forests. Eat bulbs and leaves. Cattail: Roots, shoots and young flower spikes in marshes. The roots can be pounded in water to release starch. Dandelion, wood sorrel, chickweed: Common greens. Eat sorrel in moderation. Birch and maple sap: Drink it or boil it down. Sugar maple syrup needs roughly forty parts sap to one. Summer (June to August) Wild strawberries, raspberries, blackberries: Roadsides, clearings and old fields. Lowbush blueberries: Abundant on coastal barrens and mountain ledges. Dry them in the sun to store.

"The Great Illusionist Santiago" That is what the sign said. Great may have been an overstatement, the old man reflected upon seeing the diminutive figure that set foot on stage. And yet, he had a poise about him that was difficult to place. The old man watch quietly from the back of the room as the Great Santiago pulled a rabbit from an apparently empty hat. The audience cheered loudly, but for a moment the old man began to second guess if his coming here was right after all.

He deftly slipped his hand into the pocket of his cloak and idly felt the gnarled furnishings of his all so familiar wand. For a moment, he was reassured in his quest. Something was off in this place, he felt in his bones. Faint whisperings on the wind carried tidings of ill omen; the Val Dakin had been found. If the old man were to confront a foe as powerful as this, he would rather have a mage to accompany him, or at least an alchemist. But as it were, the Great Illusionist Santiago would have to be help enough.

Convolutionary neural networks owe a large part of their success to images of the regular grid structure and translation symmetry of the plane that does not exist on curved surfaces. A common workaround map a surface to a planar domain and uses a standard CNN, but existing surface-to-image representations either large area distortion or require multiple images to cover the entire shape. We propose a new representation of ball surfaces based on general deck cards.

Instead of relying on a toric cover with a fixed set of cone points, our construction wraps a flat torus several times around the surface, so that each region with a low distortion appears somewhere in a single image. Since this image is seamless and periodic, convolution with circular padding is well defined, and off-the-shelf architectures apply with minimal modification. The predictions from the multiple copies of each surface point are then aggregated to the mesh again. Experiments with form segmentation and classification benchmarks show that the method meets or exceeds competing approaches while remaining simple and efficient.

How a Teenager's Curiosity Brought the FBI to His Door As a teenager, Timothy Winslow devoted nearly all his spare hours to a single pursuit: poking around inside computer systems. Sports and the typical teenage hangouts held no appeal for him. He was hooked instead on figuring out how networked machines operated, and he chased that puzzle all over the country, logging into systems belonging to companies, universities and institutions he had never set foot in. In his own mind, it was simply curiosity. He insists he never regarded it as a crime.

He was working out how the systems connected, following links from one computer to the next and testing how far one login could get him. "It was like a giant map that nobody had finished drawing," he remembered. And then FBI agents showed up. Their visit transformed what he considered a pastime into a grave legal problem. Under federal law, gaining unauthorized access to computer systems is a crime no matter what the person intended, and investigators could not tell whether an inquisitive teenager might also pose a danger.

"Veracity" is a thought-provoking and haunting exploration of love, trust, and the power of deception.

Channel state information (CSI) at the base station (BS) is crucial to achieve beamforming and multiplexing gains in multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems. State-of-the-art limited feedback schemes require feedback overhead that scales linearly with the number of BS antennas, which is prohibitive for 5 G massive MIMO. This work proposes novel limited feedback algorithms that lift this burden by exploiting the inherent sparsity in double directional (DD) MIMO channel representation using overcomplete dictionaries. These dictionaries are associated with angle of arrival (AoA) and angle of departure (AoD) that specifically account for antenna directivity patterns at both ends of the link.

The proposed algorithms achieve satisfactory channel estimation accuracy using a small number of feedback bits, even when the number of transmit antennas at the BS is large - making them ideal for 5 G massive MIMO. Judicious simulations reveal that they outperform a number of popular feedback schemes, and underscore the importance of using angle dictionaries matching the given antenna directivity patterns, as opposed to uniform dictionaries. The proposed algorithms are lightweight in terms of computation, especially on the user equipment side, making them ideal for actual deployment in 5 G systems.

The parrot's name was Doctor, and he was older than the marriage. Walt had bought him in 1979 from a man at a flea market who swore the bird could recite the Gettysburg Address. He couldn't. What he could do, within a month of coming home, was imitate Walt perfectly: the throat clear before a phone call, the low whistle when a pot boiled over, and above all, the sentence Walt shouted every single morning when he pulled open the kitchen curtains. "Boy, its a joyous day outside!" He said it in rain. He said it in sleet.

He said it the February the furnace died and they wore coats to breakfast. June used to roll her eyes and tell him it was eight degrees and the sky looked like dishwater, and Walt would say that was precisely what made it joyous, that any fool could be happy in sunshine. Doctor learned it in Walt's exact voice, gravel and all, and for forty-four years the two of them said it together, man and bird, while June buttered toast and pretended to be annoyed. Walt died in March.

This research article explores various methods of calculating multiple binomial sums, which are expressions involving a sum of products of binomials. The study delves into historical background and modern applications of these calculations in fields such as probability theory, combinatorics, and cryptography. Various techniques including combinatorial approaches, generating functions, and algebraic manipulations are discussed with examples to demonstrate their effectiveness. Finally, potential future directions for further exploration in this area are proposed. Overall, this comprehensive analysis provides valuable insights on efficient calculation strategies for complex polynomial equations that arise frequently in mathematical modeling problems.

Convolutional neural networks achieve much of their power on images because the plane offers a regular grid and translation symmetry, and curved surfaces have neither. A frequent workaround flattens a surface onto a planar domain so that an ordinary CNN can be used, yet current surface-to-image representations either cause heavy area distortion or need multiple images to cover an entire shape. We introduce a new representation for sphere-type surfaces built on general covering maps.

Instead of a toric cover with a fixed set of cone points, our approach has a flat torus wind around the surface several times, so each region shows up with little distortion somewhere in one image. This image is seamless and periodic, which makes convolution with circular padding well defined and lets standard architectures be used with only minor changes. Predictions from the several copies of each surface point are afterward merged back onto the mesh. On shape segmentation and classification benchmarks, the method performs on par with or better than competing approaches, and it stays simple and efficient.

On big e-commerce platforms, product feeds mix organic recommendations with sponsored listings, and ad placement has usually been tuned to bring in as much advertising revenue as possible right away. That short-term view misses an important side effect: when ads are badly placed or too numerous, users may engage less with organic content, which lowers the platform's long-term value. This paper casts the allocation of ads in product feeds as a sequential decision problem, with the goal of maximizing organic traffic subject to limits on ad exposure and revenue.

We put forward a reinforcement learning framework in which an agent decides, for each request, how many ads to insert into the feed and where, taking into account the user's context and the list of candidate items. Because engagement signals are sparse and delayed, our reward blends immediate click feedback with a learned estimate of how deeply users will browse afterward, and a constrained policy optimization scheme is used to meet platform-wide advertising targets.

When evaluating computer vision systems, we are often concerned with performance on a task-specific evaluation measure such as the Intersection-Over-Union score used in the PASCAL VOC image segmentation challenge. Ideally, our systems would be tuned specifically to these evaluation measures. However, despite much work on loss-aware structured prediction, top performing systems do not use these techniques. In this work, we seek to address this problem, incorporating loss-aware prediction in a manner that is amenable to the approaches taken by top performing systems.

Our main idea is to simultaneously leverage two systems: a highly tuned pipeline system as is found on top of leaderboards, and a traditional CRF. We show how to combine high quality candidate solutions from the pipeline with the probabilistic approach of the CRF that is amenable to loss-aware prediction. The result is that we can use loss-aware prediction methodology to improve performance of the highly tuned pipeline system.

Crowds had lined the streets in the days before as the king's coffin made its way to the city.

Richard was killed in 1485 when the forces of Henry Tudor, later Henry VII, defeated his army, effectively ending the Wars of the Roses. His grave was later lost, until the remains were unearthed in 2012 beneath a car park on the site of the former Greyfriars friary. The skeleton, its spine curved by scoliosis and its skull marked by the wounds of a violent death, was identified through DNA testing, including a match with a descendant of the king's sister.

A tactile sensor is a device that measures information arising from physical interaction with its environment. Tactile sensors are generally modeled after the biological sense of cutaneous touch which is capable of detecting stimuli resulting from mechanical stimulation, temperature, and pain (although pain sensing is not common in artificial tactile sensors). Tactile sensors are used in robotics, computer hardware and security systems. A common application of tactile sensors is in touchscreen devices on mobile phones and computing. Tactile sensors may be of different types including piezoresistive, piezoelectric, optical, capacitive and elastoresistive sensors.

Convolutional neural networks owe much of their success on images to the regular grid structure and translation symmetry of the plane, neither of which exists on curved surfaces. A common workaround maps a surface to a planar domain and applies a standard CNN, but existing surface-to-image representations either introduce large area distortion or require several images to cover the whole shape. We propose a new representation for sphere-type surfaces based on general covering maps.

Rather than relying on a toric cover with a fixed set of cone points, our construction lets a flat torus wrap around the surface several times, so that every region appears with low distortion somewhere in a single image. Because this image is seamless and periodic, convolution with circular padding is well defined, and off-the-shelf architectures apply with minimal modification. Predictions from the multiple copies of each surface point are then aggregated back onto the mesh. Experiments on shape segmentation and classification benchmarks show that the method matches or exceeds competing approaches while remaining simple and efficient.

Many people now work from home as a matter of course, and it has pros and cons. One benefit is that remote workers save time and money by skipping the commute. My mom, for instance, used to drive for more than an hour each day, and she now spends that time making dinner and helping me with my homework. Working from home also lets people set their own schedules more freely. On the downside, there are genuine drawbacks. Lots of people get lonely without coworkers nearby, and talking with a team through screens can be harder.

Home is also full of distractions such as the TV, pets, or relatives, which makes it hard to concentrate. And some people struggle to stop working when their office is in their bedroom. All in all, working from home can be wonderful, but only when people find ways to stay in touch and draw clear boundaries.

Over the past two decades, a string of critics, journalists and political rivals have been shot, poisoned or sent to prison, a pattern that human rights groups and Western governments say cannot be explained by chance. The superconducting transition leads to a sharp resistance drop in a temperature interval that can be a small fraction of the critical temperature T$c$. A superconductor exactly at T$c$ is thus very sensitive to all kinds of thermal perturbations, including the heat dissipated by the measurement current. We show that the interaction between electrical and thermal currents leads to a sizeable imaginary impedance at frequencies of order of tens of Hz at the resistive transition of single crystals of the layered material 2H-NbSe$_2$. We explain the result using models developed for transition edge sensors.
By measuring under magnetic fields and at high currents, we find that the imaginary impedance is strongly influenced by the heat associated with vortex motion and out-of-equilibrium quasiparticles.

In my last life I was Gerald Pruitt, certified public accountant, and I died at my desk on April 14th, which is the least surprising way an accountant has ever gone. For sixty-eight years, I was agreeable. I laughed at my boss's golf stories. I told my sister-in-law her tuna casserole was "really something." I said "no, no, after you" to men who deserved to wait in the rain. Then I closed my eyes over a stack of tax returns and opened them in a hospital nursery, red-faced and furious and named Tyler, with every memory intact.

It took me a while to appreciate what I'd been given. Not the knowledge. The immunity. Nobody holds a small child responsible for anything. It took five agonizing years to get my mouth working properly, and I have been making up for lost time ever since. At Aunt Denise's wedding, in that holy hush right before the vows, I tugged my mother's sleeve and asked, at a volume calibrated to reach the back pew, "Mommy, when they get divorced, who gets the boat?" At Grandpa Lou's funeral, the pastor invited anyone with a memory to come forward.

What the Mirror Kept The vaccine was supposed to end it. That was the promise: one dose, and no more winters spent counting the dead. Instead, within six weeks, it emptied the world. The lucky ones died quietly in their sleep. The rest went insane, whispering to people nobody else could see until their bodies gave out. My husband, Tomas, spent his last four days sitting in the dark bathroom, apologizing to the mirror. I should have followed him. I'd taken the same dose, in the same clinic, on the same Tuesday.

But on day forty I woke with a clear head and an apartment that still smelled like him. I avoided mirrors. I hung a bedsheet over the bathroom one and kept the rest of the apartment dark. In the abandoned houses I scavenged, I'd found the insane curled up in front of mirrors, palms flat against the glass, as if trying to climb in. A week later I ran out of excuses. I pulled down the sheet and looked. The woman in the mirror had my hair, my chipped tooth, my scar through the left eyebrow.

Should University Teach Practical Skills or Theory? A common question is what universities ought to teach. One group believes students need to learn practical skills for work. Another group believes theory matters more. In my view, each side makes good arguments. To begin with, practical skills are extremely helpful. After graduation, students have to get a job. Employers usually prefer people who can start working right away. A computer science student, for instance, should be able to write actual programs instead of just reading about them. In addition, practical courses such as internships give students real experience.

They get to know people at the company and see how an office runs. Because of this, getting a first job becomes easier. On the other hand, theory also matters. It shows students how to think. If you know why something works, you can figure out new problems on your own. Technology moves very quickly, and a skill that everyone wants now may be outdated in five years. Yet a student who understands the basic principles can pick up new tools fast. Someone who knows economic theory, for example, can understand many kinds of business jobs instead of just one.

Explicit Evidence Systems with Common Knowledge is an academic paper that explores the use of evidence-based decision making in healthcare. The paper proposes a new approach to evidence-based decision making that incorporates common knowledge into the decision-making process. The authors argue that common knowledge, which is knowledge that is widely accepted and understood by a group of people, can be a valuable source of evidence in healthcare decision making.

The paper presents a framework for incorporating common knowledge into evidence-based decision making, which involves identifying and defining common knowledge, collecting and organizing evidence related to common knowledge, and using common knowledge to inform decision making. The authors also discuss the challenges associated with incorporating common knowledge into evidence-based decision making, such as the potential for bias and the need for standardization. The paper provides several examples of how common knowledge can be used in healthcare decision making, including the use of traditional Chinese medicine and the use of complementary and alternative medicine.

A bit of both, though "rip off" is unfair. Romans openly borrowed from Greece in sculpture, philosophy, religion, and literary models, and they were happy to admit it. But they also created things the Greeks never did. Roman law is the biggest example: a systematic civil law covering contracts, property, and legal personhood, which still shapes legal systems across Europe and Latin America. In engineering, they developed concrete, perfected the arch, vault, and dome, and built aqueducts, roads, and sewers at a scale no Greek city attempted.

Satire was a Roman genre, and the codex, the ancestor of the modern book, emerged under Roman rule. Calling Greek culture "superior" is also debatable. It was different, with its own strengths, and Rome's real talent was adapting ideas into institutions that lasted.

A black-and-white (monochrome) display requires only one bit per pixel, since each pixel has two possible states: on or off. Consequently, 64,000 pixels require 64,000 bits of memory. Because one byte comprises eight bits, dividing 64,000 by 8 yields 8,000 bytes. Using the decimal convention in which one kilobyte equals 1,000 bytes, this is precisely 8 KB. Under the binary convention (1 KB = 1,024 bytes), the figure is approximately 7.8 KB, commonly rounded to 8 KB.

AlphaFold is an artificial intelligence (AI) program developed by DeepMind, a subsidiary of Alphabet, which performs predictions of protein structure. The program is designed as a deep learning system. AlphaFold AI software has had two major versions. A team of researchers that used AlphaFold 1 (2018) placed first in the overall rankings of the 13th Critical Assessment of Structure Prediction (CASP) in December 2018. The program was particularly successful at predicting the most accurate structure for targets rated as the most difficult by the competition organisers, where no existing template structures were available from proteins with a partially similar sequence.

A team that used AlphaFold 2 (2020) repeated the placement in the CASP competition in November 2020. The team achieved a level of accuracy much higher than any other group. It scored above 90 for around two-thirds of the proteins in CASP's global distance test (GDT), a test that measures the degree to which a computational program predicted structure is similar to the lab experiment determined structure, with 100 being a complete match, within the distance cutoff used for calculating GDT.

End-to-end (E2E) systems have played a more and more important role in automatic speech recognition (ASR) and achieved great performance. However, E2E systems recognize output word sequences directly with the input acoustic feature, which can only be trained on limited acoustic data. The extra text data is widely used to improve the results of traditional artificial neural network-hidden Markov model (ANN-HMM) hybrid systems. The involving of extra text data to standard E2E ASR systems may break the E2E property during decoding. In this paper, a novel modular E2E ASR system is proposed.

The modular E2E ASR system consists of two parts: an acoustic-to-phoneme (A2P) model and a phoneme-to-word (P2W) model. The A2P model is trained on acoustic data, while extra data including large scale text data can be used to train the P2W model. This additional data enables the modular E2E ASR system to model not only the acoustic part but also the language part. During the decoding phase, the two models will be integrated and act as a standard acoustic-to-word (A2W) model.

The Small House at Allington is a novel written by British author Anthony Trollope, first published between 1864 and 1867. Maya was the only person in the building who still practiced violin in front of a mirror. Every evening she'd stand in the hallway glass watching her bow arm, and the girl on the other side did exactly what she did. Right hand became left. Left became right. The oldest trick in the world. Nobody thought twice about it. Tuesday, the reflection lifted her bow half a second too early. Maya froze. The reflection froze too, but a beat later, like it had to remember. Then it blinked, and Maya hadn't. "That's not funny," Maya whispered.

The girl in the glass tilted her head. Her mouth moved. No sound, but Maya read it: Help. She put her palm on the surface. Cold. Colder than glass should be. When the reflection raised its hand, a crack of light ran between their fingers. Not ordinary light. Silvery, thin, flickering like a bad signal. Down the corridor the bathroom mirror hummed. Then the elevator. Mirrors through the walls, all at once. Like a hundred tuning forks struck at the same time. Every pane in the building shaking. Maya didn't know the physics. Nobody did.

The use of mobile phones to transfer money, make payments and access financial services has revolutionized the lives of millions of people who have never had access to traditional banking services. Particularly in emerging markets, "mobile money" means so much more than just a digital way to transact financial services. In some countries, the majority of the population lives outside of urban centers without easy access to infrastructure like transport, electricity and even roads, let alone banking. For these communities, where literacy levels tend to be lower and incomes sporadic, mobile money is truly transforming the socio-economic landscape.

Latest statistics demonstrate the tremendous growth we've seen over the past few years -- as of October 2014, there are a total of 251 live mobile money services across 88 countries. In Sub-Saharan Africa, one of the pioneering regions for mobile money, services are available in 38 out of 47 countries. And nine of these markets -- Cameroon, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Gabon, Kenya, Madagascar, Tanzania, Uganda, Zambia and Zimbabwe -- have more mobile money accounts than bank accounts, a fact that underscores the pent-up demand. Widening the mobile money market.

Imagine every time you closed your curtains, you were capturing enough solar energy to power your laptop. The technology is available, but no one's packaged it up in a handy DIY kit at your local hardware store. Solar textiles use the same technology as traditional solar panels to convert sunlight into energy. Sheila Kennedy hopes to be the first. She's not an interior designer but an architect and professor in practice at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology who is convinced that solar textiles will revolutionize the way we collect and consume power.

"I've been thinking about what happens when power and light become flexible, literally flexible," she said. She calls it "soft power," as in the "soft energy path," a term coined Amory Lovins in the 1970s as a way to describe a world where renewable energy would gradually replace the centralized grid. Later, Joseph Nye used the term "soft power" to describe the ability of persuasion, values and culture to influence change. Kennedy's work with soft power builds on both of these ideas. For her, soft power is the ability of flexible materials to convert sunlight into energy.

The graffiti, written in a French chalk quarry and dating back almost 100 years, is plain and stark. "HJ Leach. Merely a private. 13/7/16. SA Australia," reads one inscription. "HA Deanate, 148th Aero Squadron, USA. 150 Vermilyea Ave, New York City," another says. "9th Batt Australians, G. Fitzhenry, Paddington, Sydney, N.S.W., 1916 July; Alistair Ross, Lismore, July," reads a third. They were World War I soldiers, four of almost 2,000, whose writings have recently been found underneath battlefields near Naours, France, about 120 miles north of Paris.

Photographer Jeff Gusky, who has been chronicling details of the site, describes the inscriptions -- and the underground city in which they were found -- as "breathtaking." "This is a treasure trove," he said Monday night from his home in East Texas, where he works as an ER doctor.

We present A novel deep learning framework for the joint reconstruction and segmentation of the cardiac walls in 3D from CT data. The proposed method, called PC-U Net, is based on a 3D U-Net architecture with a novel loss function that combines a pixel-wise loss and a perceptual loss. The pixel-wise loss is based on the mean squared error between the predicted and the ground truth segmentation, while the perceptual loss Is based on the mean squared error between the feature Maps of the encoder and decoder parts Of the network.

The proposed method is evaluated on a dataset of 100 CT scans of the heart. the results show that the proposed method outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in terms of the Dice similarity coefficient and the Hausdorff distance. The proposed method is also shown to be robust to noise and artifacts in the CT Data. We introduce a new method of estimation of parameters in semiparametric and nonparametric models. The method is based on estimating equations that are $U$-statistics in observations. The $U$-statistics are based on higher order influence functions that extend ordinary linear influence functions of the parameter of interest, and represent higher derivatives of this parameter. For parameters for which representation cannot be perfect the method leads to a bias-variance trade-off, and results in estimators that converge at a slower than $\sqrt n$-rate. In a number of examples resulting rate can be shown to be optimal.

We are particularly interested in estimating parameters in models with a nuisance parameter of high dimension or low regularity, where the parameter of interest cannot be estimated at $\sqrt n$-rate, but we also consider efficient $\sqrt n$-estimation using novel nonlinear estimators. The general approach is applied in detail to example of estimating mean response when the response is not always observed.

We show a setup for characterising the performance of a single-photon-detector absolutely and with a accuracy better of 1%. Although the setup does not rely on calibrated devices and can be implemented with standard-optic systems, it can be realised in any laboratory. Our method is based on an Erbium-Doped-Fiber-Amplifier (EDFA) radiometer as a primary measurement standard for optical power, and on an ultra-stable source of spontaneous emission. As a proof of concept, we characterise the performance of an InGaAs/InP single-photon detection. We verified the accuracy of the characterisation with independent observations.

In particular, the calculation of the optical power made with the EDFA radiometer has been compared to that of the Austrian National Department of Metrology using a transfer energy meter. Our method is useful for frequent characterisations of high-efficient single-photon detectors.

In this paper, we present a novel approach to image segmentation and representation called Superpixel Hierarchy. Our method is based on the idea of recursively partitioning an image into smaller regions, called superpixels, until a desired level of detail is reached. Each superpixel is defined by its spatial extent and set of features that capture its characteristics. We propose hierarchical framework for constructing superpixels, which allows us to efficiently represent images at multiple scales and resolutions. We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets and compare it to state-of-the-art methods in terms of segmentation accuracy and computational efficiency.

Our results show that Superpixel Hierarchy outperforms existing methods in both aspects, providing a more accurate and efficient way to segment and represent images. Additionally, we demonstrate the versatility of our approach by applying it to various computer vision tasks, such as object recognition, scene understanding, and image restoration. The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows: We introduce the concept of Superpixel Hierarchy, novel approach to image segmentation and representation that combines benefits of both pixel-based and region-based methods.

> The rapid urban expansion is a global phenomenon that has been observed in many countries. The prediction of urban expansion is a challenging task due to the complexity of the urban expansion process. In this paper, we propose a novel deep learning-based approach to predict urban expansion. The proposed approach consists of two main components: a convolutional neural network (CNN) and a long short-term memory (LSTM) network. The CNN is used to extract spatial features from the input data, and the LSTM is used to capture the temporal dependencies.

The proposed approach is evaluated on two real-world datasets from China and the United States. The experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and F1 score. I think the question, as worded, has some incorrect assumptions built into it, but let me try to hit the key answers that I think might help: Your broker can't really do anything here. Your broker doesn't own the calls you sold, and can't elect to exercise someone else's calls. Your broker can take action to liquidate positions when you are in margin calls, but the scenario you describe wouldn't generate them: If you are long stock, and short calls, the calls are covered, and have no margin requirement.

The stock is the only collateral you need, and you can have the position on in a cash (non-margin) account. So, assuming you haven't bought other things on margin that have gone south and are generating calls, your broker has no right to do anything to you. If you're wondering about the "other guy", meaning the person who is long the calls that you are short, they are the one who can impact you, by exercising their right to buy the stock from you.

This paper investigates best and worst case permutations for random online domination of path. The study focuses on the online version of domination game, where the player's objective is to minimize number of dominators. The paper presents comprehensive analysis of the game on paths, identifying the best and worst case permutations and providing a detailed explanation of the strategies leading to these outcomes. The results reveal that the worst case scenario occurs when the vertices are presented in increasing order of their distances from endpoints, while best case scenario occurs when they are presented in decreasing order.
The findings contribute to a deeper understanding of game's complexity and offer valuable insights for developing more efficient strategies.

A semi-blind watermarking scheme is presented based on Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), which makes essential use of the fact that, the SVD subspace preserves significant amount of information of an image and is a one way decomposition. The principal components are used, along with the corresponding singular vectors of the watermark image to watermark the target image. For further security, the semi-blind scheme is extended to an invisible hash based watermarking scheme. The hash based scheme commits a watermark with a key such that, it is incoherent with the actual watermark, and can only be extracted using the key.
Its security is analyzed in the random oracle model and shown to be unforgeable, invisible and satisfying the property of non-repudiation.

Detecting early signs of failures (anomalies) in complex systems is one of the main goal of preventive maintenance. It allows in particular to avoid actual failures by (re) scheduling maintenance operations in a way that optimizes maintenance costs. Aircraft engine health monitoring is one representative example of a field in which anomaly detection is crucial. Manufacturers collect large amount of engine related data during flights which are used, among other applications, to detect anomalies.

This article introduces and studies a generic methodology that allows one to build automatic early signs of anomaly detection in a way that builds upon human expertise and that remains understandable by human operators who make the final maintenance decision. The main idea of the method is to generate a very large number of binary indicators based on parametric anomaly scores designed by experts, complemented by simple aggregations of those scores. A feature selection method is used to keep only the most discriminant indicators which are used as inputs of a Naive Bayes classifier.

> We propose an approach to quantum cryptography that goes beyond quantum key distribution (QKD). In particular, we show how to use quantum mechanics to achieve unconditionally secure authentication and signatures in addition to encryption. Our protocols are based on the idea of using entanglement as а resource rather than just single qubits. This allows us to construct schemes with security proofs against general attacks by adversaries who have access to any number of copies of the shared entangled state. Furthermore, our constructions can be implemented without requiring any trusted parties or additional assumptions such as device-independence.

We present results for collisional energy loss and momentum broadening of high momentum partons in a hot and dense non-Abelian plasma obtained by solving the coupled system of Yang-Mills-Wong equations on a lattice in real time. Including hard elastic collisions among the particles we obtain cutoff independent results for the collisional energy loss dE/dx and the transport coefficient q-hat. The latter is found to receive a sizable contribution from a power-law tail in the transverse momentum distribution of high-momentum partons.

We further argue that the effect of instabilities on jet broadening should be accessible by experiment when employing jet cones with elliptical bases or studying correlations within the cone in full jet reconstruction methods.

Richard III Laid to Rest Again in Leicester as Cumberbatch Delivers Tribute King Richard III was finally reburied on Thursday at Leicester Cathedral, five hundred years after he died at the Battle of Bosworth, in a ceremony that combined medieval pageantry with modern celebrity. Richard, the last Plantagenet king, was killed in 1485 and buried in a hurry in the church of the Greyfriars friary in Leicester. In the following centuries the site was built over and its location was lost.

Then in 2012 archaeologists made a stunning discovery, finding his remains under a city council car park, and DNA tests against descendants of his sister later confirmed the identification. On Thursday, 530 years after the king's death, his oak coffin was lowered into a grave inside the cathedral. Actor Benedict Cumberbatch, a distant cousin of Richard, was one of the participants, reading a poem that Poet Laureate Carol Ann Duffy had written for the occasion. Historian Philippa Langley, whose campaign set the search for the grave in motion, said the find had led researchers to reconsider the king.

The capacity of finite state channels (FSCs) has been established as the limit of a sequence of multi-letter expressions only and, despite tremendous effort, a corresponding finite-letter characterization remains unknown to date. This paper analyzes the capacity of FSCs from a fundamental, algorithmic point of view by studying whether or not the corresponding achievability and converse bounds on the capacity can be computed algorithmically. For this purpose, the concept of Turing machines is used which provide the fundamental performance limits of digital computers.

To this end, computable continuous functions are studied and properties of computable sequences of such functions are identified. It is shown that the capacity of FSCs is not Banach-Mazur computable which is the weakest form of computability. This implies that there is no algorithm (or Turing machine) that can compute the capacity of a given FSC. As a consequence, it is then shown that either the achievability or converse must yield a bound that is not Banach-Mazur computable. This also means that there exist FSCs for which computable lower and upper bounds can never be tight.

FeSe enters a nematic phase near 90 K without any long-range magnetic order, which makes it an ideal system for isolating the electronic origin of rotational symmetry breaking in iron-based superconductors. We use high-resolution angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy on mechanically detwinned single crystals to map how the electronic structure changes across the nematic transition, resolved by momentum and orbital. At low temperature, the dxz/dyz splitting at the Brillouin zone corner reaches roughly 50 meV, setting the characteristic nematic energy scale, whereas the splitting near the zone center is much smaller, which points to a strongly momentum-dependent order parameter.

Remarkably, the nematic state shows just one electron pocket; the pocket expected at the Y point cannot be detected within our experimental resolution. We examine how orbital-selective correlations and the d_xy orbital contribute to this suppression, and we argue that the resulting anisotropic Fermi surface naturally explains both the strongly anisotropic superconducting gap and the lack of magnetic order in FeSe.

Whether it's a weekend barbecue or roasting marshmallows on a camping trip, cooking over an open fire is a novelty that many Americans enjoy. But for nearly half the world's population, building and maintaining a fire is a daily -- and often deadly -- chore. In remote villages and city slums, women tend to fires for hours on end, breathing in smoke that is the equivalent of smoking two packs of cigarettes a day, according to the World Health Organization.

Many of these women have their children close by or strapped to their chest or back, and the dangerous pollutants from the smoke can result in severe damage to their lungs as well. Nancy Hughes witnessed this firsthand while working with a medical team in Guatemala more than a decade ago. "There were doctors on the medical team who could not put tubes down the babies' throats because the throats were so choked with creosote," said Hughes, a 70-year-old grandmother who lives in Eugene, Oregon.
Both, really.

The Romans borrowed openly from Greece, and they knew it: Horace wrote that "captive Greece took her savage conqueror captive." But they also contributed plenty that was genuinely their own: - Law: A systematic legal tradition with professional jurists and concepts of contracts, property, and citizens' rights that still underpins civil law across Europe and Latin America. - Engineering: Concrete construction that made vast vaults and domes like the Pantheon possible, plus aqueducts, sewers, and a road network spanning the Mediterranean. - Governance: Running a multiethnic empire for centuries while gradually extending citizenship to conquered peoples. - Literature and art: Verse satire, which Quintilian proudly called "wholly ours," and a distinctive tradition of unflinchingly realistic portrait busts.

In situations where establishing a network infrastructure is impossible, Ad-hoc networks are considered particularly important. Most of the previous research in Ad-hoc networks concentrated on the development and enhancement of dynamic routing protocols, which could efficiently discover routes between two communicating nodes. Although routing strategies is an important topic in MANETs, other topics such as data access are also crucial since the final goal of using Ad-hoc networks is to provide data access to mobile nodes.

One of the most attractive techniques used to improve the data access performance in MANET environment is cooperative caching; which means multiple caching nodes share and cooperatively manage the cached contents. It is lead the research to important questions, what data should be cached, where, when, and how? A cooperative caching addressed into two basic issues: cache discovery and cache management, in other words, how to find requested data efficiently and how to manage an individual cache to improve the overall capacity of a cooperated cache.

Obama pushed hard for fast-track authority (formally, Trade Promotion Authority) on the Trans-Pacific Partnership for a few interconnected reasons. Getting the deal done at all. Fast-track lets Congress vote yes or no on a trade agreement without amending it. Other countries, especially Japan, were reluctant to make final concessions if Congress could later rewrite the terms. Without TPA, negotiators believed the TPP would likely collapse. Geopolitics and China.

The administration framed TPP as central to its "pivot to Asia." Obama argued that if the U.S. didn't help write the rules for trade in the Asia-Pacific, China would, on terms less favorable to American workers and businesses. Economic goals. The deal would cut tariffs on U.S. exports, set standards for intellectual property and digital trade, and include labor and environmental provisions stronger than earlier agreements like NAFTA. Legacy. TPP was a signature second-term initiative. The push was notable because most opposition came from Obama's own party, so he worked with Republican leaders to pass TPA in 2015.

It happened on a Tuesday, which seemed unfair. Gods shouldn't have to remember things on Tuesdays. I was standing in the grocery store checkout—holding eggs and a laundry detergent coupon—when it hit me. Not like a thought. Like remembering your own phone number. Oh. Right. I'm God. The stars, the platypus, that weird orange on the fruit stand across the aisle. All me. I'd just stepped away for a while. The woman in front of me was arguing with the cashier about a banana. Not the price, just the banana.

And something opened up in my chest so huge my knees buckled. I knew exactly how many hairs she had. I knew she cried in her car that morning. I dropped the eggs. Twelve of them, all over the floor. "Sir? You okay?" "I made you," I said. It came out gentler than I meant, way scarier than I wanted. She stepped back. The banana woman stared. The kid at the next register was reaching for his phone. Ten seconds. Ten seconds before a video. Here's what I understood in those ten seconds. Being God isn't like being a king.

The Office on the Fourteenth Floor Dr. Eleanor Vance maintained her practice in an unremarkable building downtown, between a dental surgery and an accounting firm. Her nameplate listed no specialty. Referrals arrived by word of mouth, through channels that she had learned not to question. Her nine o'clock on Monday was a man who had once attempted to flood a coastal city. He sat in the armchair across from her, removed his gloves with deliberate care, and spoke for forty minutes about his father. "He told me the ocean would take everything eventually," the man said.

"I suppose I wished to prove him right on my own schedule." Dr. Vance made a note. She did not write the word villain in her files. She had abandoned that term early in her career, after realizing it described an outcome rather than a person. Her clients had committed terrible acts; several remained capable of committing more. Her work was not to absolve them. It was to understand what had brought them to the threshold, and whether any of them might still be persuaded to step back.

Optical static random access memory (O-SRAM) is one of the key components required for achieving the goal of ultra-fast, general-purpose optical computing. We propose and design a novel O-SRAM using fabrication-friendly photonics device components such as cross-coupled micro-ring resonators and photodiodes. Based on the chosen photonic components, the memory operates at a speed of 20 Gb/s and requires ultra-low static (switching) energy of ~ 16.7 aJ/bit (~ 1.04 pJ/bit) to store a single bit. The footprint of the bit cell is ~ 2400 {\mu}m^2.

The proposed O-SRAM can be configured in a 2D memory array by replicating the bit-cells along rows and columns for creating ultra-large scale on-chip optical memory sub-system. Such manufacturing-friendly, large-scale optical-SRAM could form the underlying memory backbone for photonics integrated circuits with wide applications in novel computing and networking.

We study the problem of learning the transition matrices of a set of Markov chains from a single stream of observations on each chain. We assume that the Markov chains are ergodic but otherwise unknown. The learner can sample Markov chains sequentially to observe their states. The goal of the learner is to sequentially select various chains to learn transition matrices uniformly well with respect to some loss function.

We introduce a notion of loss that naturally extends the squared loss for learning distributions to the case of Markov chains, and further characterize the notion of being uniformly good in all problem instances. We present a novel learning algorithm that efficiently balances exploration and exploitation intrinsic to this problem, without any prior knowledge of the chains. We provide finite-sample PAC-type guarantees on the performance of the algorithm. Further, we show that our algorithm asymptotically attains an optimal loss.

Polar-ring galaxies have a central early-type host, usually an S0 or elliptical, surrounded by a ring or disk of gas, dust, and young stars that orbits in a plane nearly perpendicular to the host's major axis. How they form is still debated. Proposed explanations include tidal accretion of material from a passing companion, cold gas accretion along cosmic filaments, and major mergers. We present high-resolution N-body/hydrodynamical simulations of an unequal-mass merger between two gas-rich disk galaxies, with an orbital configuration that favors a polar structure.

We find that gas from the disrupted companion settles into a stable, self-gravitating ring orthogonal to the remnant within about 1 Gyr, while the stellar components relax into a spheroidal host. The resulting system reproduces the morphology, kinematics, and ring-to-host mass ratio seen in prototypical objects such as NGC 4650A. We discuss the conditions needed and how often polar rings built by mergers should be expected.

ZTE Corp obtained and illegally shipped US-made equipment to Iran in violation of US sanctions, the Justice Department said. It also sent goods to North Korea without the correct export licences. The US said ZTE lied to authorities and its own lawyer about the violations. It must now pay a 892m (PS740m) penalty as well as 300m which will be suspended for seven years depending on the firm meeting certain conditions. ZTE says it acknowledges it has made mistakes, and is working towards improving its procedures.

The US said that the highest levels of management at ZTE approved the scheme which involved the shipment of 32m worth of US-made goods to Iran between 2010 and 2016. The equipment included routers, microprocessors and servers controlled under export regulations for "security, encryption... andor anti-terrorism reasons." ZTE also made 283 shipments of mobile phones to North Korea despite knowing this contravened rules around exports to the country. According to Reuters, ZTE buys around a third of its its components from US businesses such as Qualcomm, Microsoft and Intel.

Claims such as "four out of five dentists recommend" are typically based on genuine surveys, but the wording often overstates what was actually measured. A company or its research contractor may poll a sample of dental professionals, sometimes a few hundred, and ask which brands they would recommend. Crucially, respondents are frequently permitted to name several brands. Consequently, 80 percent of dentists may include a particular toothpaste on their list while recommending competitors just as often. In 2007, the UK Advertising Standards Authority ruled that a Colgate advertisement using this type of claim was misleading for precisely this reason.

The statistic, therefore, does not usually mean that dentists prefer your toothpaste over all others. It generally indicates only that most surveyed dentists consider it an acceptable option, which is true of most fluoride toothpastes.

Abstract. Quantifying model uncertainty is a central problem in the statistical analysis of complex systems, particularly when observed data depart from Gaussian assumptions. Conventional approaches typically rely on Gaussian approximations or on measures that are sensitive to heavy tails and skewness. In this work, we propose a framework that uses the Hellinger distance to assess the discrepancy between candidate models and the distribution of non-Gaussian observations. Because the Hellinger distance is bounded and symmetric, it offers stable comparisons across models with differing supports and tail behavior.

We derive estimators for the distance based on observed data, establish their consistency under mild conditions, and describe how the resulting values may be used to rank models and to construct uncertainty bounds. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that the proposed method detects model misspecification more reliably than comparable Gaussian-based measures. The results indicate that the Hellinger distance provides a robust and interpretable tool for uncertainty quantification in non-Gaussian settings.

Background: The trend towards large-scale studies including population imaging poses new challenges in terms of quality control (QC). This is a particular issue when automatic processing tools, e.g. image segmentation methods, are employed to derive quantitative measures or biomarkers for later analyses. Manual inspection and visual QC of each segmentation isn't feasible at large scale. However, it's important to be able to automatically detect when a segmentation method fails so as to avoid inclusion of wrong measurements into subsequent analyses which could lead to incorrect conclusions.

Methods: To overcome this challenge, we explore an approach for predicting segmentation quality based on Reverse Classification Accuracy, which enables us to discriminate between successful and failed segmentations on a per-cases basis. We validate this approach on a new, large-scale manually-annotated set of 4,800 cardiac magnetic resonance scans. We then apply our method to a large cohort of 7,250 cardiac MRI on which we have performed manual QC. Results: We report results used for predicting segmentation quality metrics including Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) and surface-distance measures.

Hard scattering angles are sensitive to gluon polarization in unpolarized hadrons. This polarization comes from perturbative effects, so it can create azimuthal modulations like cos 2φ in events with heavy quarks, dijets, and Higgs. The upper limit is set by positivity bounds, and people thought it could be pretty big. We looked at how soft gluon radiation affects this. When we resum large logarithms between the hard scale and pair transverse momentum, we found Sudakov suppression kills the polarized component much harder than the unpolarized one.

So the asymmetries end up way below the maximum at kinematics where the factorized description works. We worked out the suppression for LHC kinematics and future electron-ion collider energies, showing how it depends on the hard scale and nonperturbative input. Earlier estimates were too optimistic. It turns out some observables still have real sensitivity to gluon polarization, but not as much as people thought.

This paper discusses Ramsey-type equations for lines in 3-dimensional space. It delves into the geometric concept of Ramsey, which states that given enough objects, some particular structure will eventually emerge. The paper expands this notion to lines in 3-space, giving a detailed study of the circumstances under which such types occur. The study subsequently provides many new findings, including a proof of a Ramsey-type theory for lines in 3-space. These results contribute to our knowledge of computational topology and have potential applications in areas such as computer graphics and visual information analysis.

Sony has revealed the cell, the long-awaited new processor for the upcoming PS3 game console, which promises an enormous leap in performance. The new chip was developed together with IBM and Toshiba and promises to provide a performance of two teraflops, which is about 40 times faster than the current PS2 chip. The cell is a multi-core chip, which combines a general-purpose PowerPC core with eight specialized "vector" coprocessors. This combination of architectural concepts allows the PS3 to perform several tasks at once and thus offers a more realistic and more involving game experience.

The choice of the cell as the new chip for the PS3 therefore represents a significant change from the 'Emotion Engine' of the PS2 which, by the way, is itself a revision of the Emotion Engine. The cell is designed to process complex calculations and is thus particularly suitable for the high-resolution graphics and complex physics simulations that modern games demand. The cell is also equipped with a network connection that will allow the PS3 to offer a wide range of network services, such as high-resolution streaming videos and the possibility of accessing game content via the Internet.

Friday night. Me, Priya, and Marcus hunched over a huge pepperoni pizza in the office, pretending we weren't going to touch the production server. "Nobody touches anything," Marcus said, grease on his hand. "We eat, we go home." Then the dashboard went red. Every line spiked at once. Priya leaned in. "That can't be right. Four million requests per second?" "We have forty users," I said. "Then someone's really popular." She grabbed a slice and kept staring. We traced it to a test box in the corner we called Zombie—thing's been decommissioned three times and keeps coming back.

Someone had left it plugged in. It was hammering our staging environment with requests from a script nobody could find. "Kill it," Marcus said. "Can't SSH in. It's not on the network." "It's obviously on the network." "The dashboard says the network. The dashboard also thinks it's 1970." Priya was already under the desk. "There's an ethernet cable here. Yellow. Why's it yellow?" "Nobody knows," Marcus said gravely. "It's always been yellow." She traced it with her hand like defusing a bomb.

Women have been badly let down by the men they stood with during demonstrations that toppled tyrants in the Middle East and North Africa. Shot at, tortured, assaulted and detained -- they were equals at the point of protest but now, as new governments extend their grip, we can see that, as citizens, women remain firmly in the second class. So, as we celebrate the role of women on International Women's day, let us not forget that the struggle for equality is far from won.

Even when progress seems to be a given, the pendulum can swing back leaving fresh challenges to defend progressive values. In Egypt, it did not matter that women had played a critical role in the uprisings that ousted the tyrant Mubarak. It did not matter that they had suffered equally from repression and lack of economic opportunity along with the men. It did not matter that they were subjected to the additional burden of discrimination because they were female.

The question "how many squares are on a chessboard?" has two answers. Count only the 64 small light and dark cells and you get 64. Count every square you could outline on the board, large ones built from smaller cells included, and the figure rises to 204. Squares of every size Beyond the 64 single cells, the 8 × 8 grid hides squares measuring 2 × 2, 3 × 3, and so on, all the way to the whole board, which counts as a single 8 × 8 square. What matters is how many places each size can sit.
Start with 2 × 2. Its upper-left corner may fall in any of the first 7 columns and any of the first 7 rows, giving 7 × 7 = 49 squares.

Tomasz Imieliński (born July 11, 1954 in Toruń, Poland) is a Polish-American computer scientist, most known in the areas of data mining, mobile computing, data extraction, and search engine technology. He is currently a professor of computer science at Rutgers University in New Jersey, United States. In 2000, he co-founded Connotate Technologies, a web data extraction company based in New Brunswick, NJ. Since 2004 till 2010 he had held multiple positions at Ask.com, from vice president of data solutions intelligence to executive vice president of global search and answers and chief scientist.

From 2010 to 2012 he served as VP of data solutions at IAC/Pronto. Tomasz Imieliński served as chairman of the Computer Science Department at Rutgers University from 1996 to 2003. He co-founded Art Data Laboratories LLC company, and its product, Articker is the largest known database that aggregates dynamic non-price information about the visual artists in the global art market. Articker has been under an exclusive partnership with Phillips auction house.[10][11][12][13]

Reaching for the Stars Without Neglecting Home Every year, governments spend billions on rockets, probes, and telescopes, while millions of people lack clean water, healthcare, or schooling. It is easy to see why critics argue that this money belongs on Earth. Yet treating space exploration and earthly problems as rivals misunderstands how both progress. The case against space spending is emotionally powerful. A single Mars mission could fund hospitals or vaccination campaigns. When people suffer now, spending on distant planets can seem like a luxury for wealthy nations. However, space budgets are smaller than many assume.

NASA receives less than half a percent of the U.S. federal budget, a fraction of what goes to defense or health programs. More importantly, space research repays its cost in practical ways. Satellites track hurricanes, monitor crops, and measure climate change. Technologies first developed for spaceflight have led to improvements in water purification, medical imaging, and solar power. Space programs also inspire students to pursue science and engineering. Governments should therefore continue funding space exploration, but wisely: prioritizing missions with clear scientific or social value and cooperating internationally to share costs.
