The world learned his name after he was killed by a South Carolina police officer. But in his life, 50-year-old Walter Scott was also the father of four children and served in the Coast Guard before being honorably discharged. "He was outgoing -- loved everybody, (was) very known in the community and got along with everybody," his brother Anthony Scott told CNN's Don Lemon. "All the family loves him, and his kids loved him." Until it all came crashing down Saturday morning, when North Charleston police Officer Michael Slager pulled Scott over, reportedly for a faulty brake light.

Dash cam video released Thursday shows the two talking, then shows Scott get out of his car and run. Why did he run? Justin Bamberg, a lawyer for Scott's family, speculated Thursday it could have been related to "child support and a fear of maybe going back to (jail)." At the time of his death, Scott owed over $18,000 in back payments for two children and hadn't made a payment since July 2012, according to Charleston County family court documents.

Current top-performing blind perceptual image quality prediction models are generally trained on legacy databases of human quality opinion scores on synthetically distorted images. Therefore they learn image features that effectively predict human visual quality judgments of inauthentic, and usually isolated (single) distortions. However, real-world images usually contain complex, composite mixtures of multiple distortions. We study the perceptually relevant natural scene statistics of such authentically distorted images, in different color spaces and transform domains.

We propose a bag of feature-maps approach which avoids assumptions about the type of distortion(s) contained in an image, focusing instead on capturing consistencies, or departures therefrom, of the statistics of real world images. Using a large database of authentically distorted images, human opinions of them, and bags of features computed on them, we train a regressor to conduct image quality prediction.

"kWh/kW" works out to hours. A kilowatt-hour (kWh) is an amount of energy, and a kilowatt (kW) is a rate of power, so dividing energy by power gives time. In practice, the ratio often describes how many hours a system would need to run at full power to produce a given amount of energy. For solar installations, annual kWh per kW of installed capacity measures yield, and it's closely related to capacity factor.

Figures for England, Wales and Northern Ireland showed more than a quarter of cases were not picked up within the required 24 hours after birth. Health campaigners say the problem can affect crucial early days of bonding. A cleft palate is a gap in the roof of the mouth leading to difficulties sucking adequately and trouble feeding. The condition can also lead to hearing and speech difficulties, and may indicate other problems with the heart or nervous system. Unlike a cleft lip, a cleft in the palate is hard to identify in a scan during pregnancy.

National guidelines say the problem, which affects about 500 babies every year in the UK, should be diagnosed within 24 hours of birth. This allows quick referral to a team of experts including surgeons, nurses, orthodontists and speech and language therapists. But figures published by the Royal College of Surgeons show a cleft palate is often missed at birth. They come from the Crane Database, which is a national register of information on those born with a cleft lip or palate in England, Wales and Northern Ireland.

Population atlases of brain and spinal cord anatomy are essential for spatial normalization, morphometric analysis, and the study of neurological disease, yet most existing atlases treat the brain and spinal cord separately and are built with deterministic registration that offers limited insight into anatomical variability. We present a generative framework for diffeomorphic atlas construction that jointly models the brain and cervical spinal cord from MRI data.

The method represents each subject as a smooth, invertible deformation of a shared template and learns both the template and a probabilistic model of deformations within a variational inference setting, implemented with a convolutional neural network. This formulation enables efficient registration of new subjects, sampling of plausible anatomical variants, and quantification of uncertainty in the estimated deformations. We evaluate the approach on multi-subject T1- and T2-weighted MRI datasets, demonstrating improved alignment of anatomical structures, preserved topology, and substantially reduced computation time compared with conventional iterative atlas-building methods.

Feeds of products on big e-commerce platforms mix organic recommendations with sponsored items, and ads have usually been positioned to maximize immediate advertising revenue. This focus on the short term ignores an important side effect: badly placed or too many ads can reduce how much users engage with organic content, which lowers the platform's value over time. In this paper, we cast ad allocation in product feeds as a sequential decision problem, aiming to maximize organic traffic subject to limits on ad exposure and revenue.

We present a reinforcement learning framework where an agent decides, for every request, how many ads to place in the feed and where, based on the user's context and the list of candidate items. Because engagement signals are sparse and delayed, we build a reward that blends immediate click feedback with a learned estimate of how deeply users browse afterward, and we use a constrained policy optimization method to meet platform-wide ad targets.

Victor Crane had never apologized for anything, and he had built a long career out of things that deserved apologies. He ran a debt collection agency the way some men run dogfights. He enjoyed the moment on a phone call when a voice cracked. He kept a ledger, not of money but of the people he had made cry, and on slow evenings he reread it over a glass of bourbon. When his own heart began to fail at fifty-eight, he took it as an insult rather than a warning. The transplant came on a Tuesday in March.

The donor was Lena, a twenty-six-year-old hospice volunteer who had been hit by a delivery van while biking to work. Victor learned this from a hospital pamphlet about writing thank-you letters to donor families. He threw it away. The first sign was small. Three weeks after surgery, a nurse dropped a tray of instruments. Normally Victor would have made a remark sharp enough to draw blood. This time he said nothing, and his chest tightened. He blamed rejection, scar tissue, the medication. His cardiologist said the heart was performing beautifully. Then he went back to the office.

Space Exploration or Problems on Earth? Many people ask if governments should spend money on space exploration. Some people think this money should be used to solve problems on Earth, like hunger, sickness and poverty. I think both sides have good points, but I believe governments should spend a small part of their money on space, and most of it on problems here. First, I understand why people are against space spending. Every day, many people in the world do not have enough food or clean water. Hospitals in poor countries often does not have enough doctors or medicine.

When I see this, it is hard to say that sending a rocket to Mars is more important. Rockets are very expensive, and one launch can cost hundreds of millions of dollars. This money could build many schools or clinics. However, space exploration also gives us many benefits. For example, scientists who work on space projects invented many things we use every day. Some of the issues you may face: A person with both Medicare and a QHP would potentially have primary coverage from 2 sources: Medicare and the QHP. No federal law addresses this situation. Under state insurance law an individual generally cannot collect full benefits from each of 2 policies that together pay more than an insured event costs.

State law usually specifies how insurance companies will coordinate health benefits when a person has primary coverage from more than one source. In that situation, insurance companies determine which coverage is primary and which is secondary. Gunmen Kill at Least 23 at Tunisia's Bardo Museum TUNIS, Tunisia — Gunmen burst into the Bardo National Museum in the Tunisian capital on Wednesday and killed at least 23 people, striking at one of the nation's most famous cultural sites and at the tourism industry that its economy relies on. The majority of the victims were foreign tourists, a number of whom had disembarked that morning from cruise ships moored in Tunis. Security forces brought a standoff inside the museum to an end by killing two of the assailants, and dozens of people received treatment for injuries.

The Bardo, home to one of the finest collections of Roman mosaics anywhere, stands beside the national parliament. The assault has rattled a country frequently called the lone success story of the Arab Spring. Following the 2011 revolution that drove out President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali, Tunisia wrote a new constitution and held free elections. But it has also become a leading supplier of foreign fighters to extremist groups in Syria and Iraq, where an estimated 3,000 Tunisians are thought to have gone.

The number of spatially unresolved white dwarf plus main-sequence star binaries has increased rapidly in the last decade, jumping from only ~30 in 2003 to over 3000. However, in the majority of known systems the companion to the white dwarf is a low mass M dwarf, since these are relatively easy to identify from optical colours and spectra. White dwarfs with more massive FGK type companions have remained elusive due to the large difference in optical brightness between the two stars.

In this paper we identify 934 main-sequence FGK stars from the Radial Velocity Experiment (RAVE) survey in the southern hemisphere and the Large Sky Area Multi-Object Fiber Spectroscopic Telescope (LAMOST) survey in the northern hemisphere, that show excess flux at ultraviolet wavelengths which we interpret as the likely presence of a white dwarf companion. We obtained Hubble Space Telescope ultraviolet spectra for nine systems which confirmed that the excess is indeed caused, in all cases, by a hot compact companion, eight being white dwarfs and one a hot subdwarf or pre-helium white dwarf, demonstrating that this sample is very clean.

The claim "four out of five dentists recommend" is a marketing statement, and its meaning depends on how the underlying survey was conducted. Companies do sometimes survey dentists, but the sample is often small, and the question is frequently phrased loosely. Respondents may be asked whether they would recommend a product, or they may be allowed to name several brands, which means that many brands can each claim to be endorsed by most dentists. The figure therefore does not necessarily indicate that 80 percent of dentists prefer that toothpaste above all others.
Consumers should look for the sample size, the exact wording of the question, and evidence of independent approval, such as the seal of a recognized dental association.

In this paper, we propose a simple and general framework for training very tiny CNNs (e.g. VGG with the number of channels reduced to 1 32) for object detection. Due to limited representation ability, it is challenging to train very tiny networks for complicated tasks like detection. To the best of our knowledge, our method, called Quantization Mimic, is the first one focusing on very tiny networks. We utilize two types of acceleration methods: mimic and quantization. Mimic improves the performance of a student network by transfering knowledge from a teacher network.

Quantization converts a full-precision network to a quantized one without large degradation of performance. If the teacher network is quantized, the search scope of the student network will be smaller. Using this feature of the quantization, we propose Quantization Mimic. It first quantizes the large network, then mimic a quantized small network. The quantization operation can help student network to better match the feature maps from teacher network. To evaluate our approach, we carry out experiments on various popular CNNs including VGG and Resnet, as well as different detection frameworks including Faster R-CNN and R-FCN.

The first night, he woke to an ache so sharp that he reached for the call button.

It wasn't in his chest. It was something else, a heaviness he couldn't place. Then he remembered Mrs. Alvarez, the widow whose shop he had driven out of business to build a parking lot. He had laughed when she cried. Now, with his pulse tapping against his ribs, he could not remember why it had seemed funny. "Phantom pain," the doctor told him. "Anxiety. It's common." But it kept coming. Each time he thought of cruelty, he felt it in his body, a tightening and a heat behind his eyes.

Working from Home: A Mixed Blessing In recent years, remote work has gone from an occasional privilege to a routine way of life for millions of people. The shift offers genuine advantages, but it also raises problems that employees and companies alike have to take seriously. Cutting out the commute is the most visible gain. Someone who used to sit in traffic for an hour in each direction recovers about ten hours every week, which can be spent with family, on exercise, or simply resting.

Working remotely is also more flexible: people can build their schedule around the hours when they work best or around obligations like looking after children or aging parents. Companies, for their part, save on office expenses and can recruit from a far larger geographic pool, because they are no longer restricted to candidates who live close by. Still, there are serious downsides to working from home. Isolation is a common complaint, as workers lose the informal chats and feeling of belonging that a shared workplace provides. Over time this can hurt mental health and erode relationships within a team.

The parrot was called Doctor, and he had been around longer than the marriage. Walt had picked him up in 1979 from a man at a flea market, who promised the bird could recite the Gettysburg Address. He could not. But within a month of arriving home, he could do Walt perfectly: the throat-clearing before a phone call, the soft whistle when a pot was about to boil over, and most of all, the line Walt hollered each morning as he yanked open the kitchen curtains. "Boy, its a joyous day outside!" He said it when it rained.

He said it when it sleeted. He said it the February the furnace broke and they ate breakfast in their coats. June would roll her eyes and point out that it was eight degrees and the sky looked like dishwater, and Walt would reply that this was exactly what made it joyous, since any fool could be happy when the sun was out. Doctor picked it up in Walt's own voice, gravel included, and for forty-four years the pair of them, man and bird, shouted it together while June buttered toast and acted annoyed. Walt died in March.

We present a model for steady state winds of systems with super-Eddington luminosities. These radiatively driven winds are expected to be optically thick and clumpy as they arise from an instability driven porous atmosphere. The model is then applied to derive the mass loss observed in bright classical novae. The main results are: 1) A general relation between the mass loss rate and the total luminosity in super-Eddington systems. 2) A quantitative agreement between the observed luminosity evolution which is used to predict both the mass loss and temperature evolution, and their observations.

3) An agreement between the predicted average integrated mass loss of novae as a function of WD mass and its observations. 4) A natural explanation for the `transition phase' of novae. 5) Agreement with eta Carinae which was used to double check the theory. The prediction for the mass shed in the star's great eruption agrees with observations to within the measurement error.

> We introduce explicit evidence systems, which provide an algorithmic version of Fuzzy Inference System (FIS). Compared to other forms of explanation of the output behaviour of blackbox models such as Partial Dependence plots (PDP), Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) and Rule List based method (RLB); our proposal has several advantages. Firstly, PDP provides marginal contribution towards а target variable instead of а specific instance as considered in case of LIME and RLB. Secondly, we focus on binary classifiers that return exact value unlike PDP and LIME that work for continuous targets only.

Thirdly, our explication of the model predictions are not driven by data points but rather they can be easily visualized using logical graph like structures. Last but certainly not least, it works well both offline and online scenarios where explanatory power is necessary е.g when user wants to have more confidence regarding what caused а particular system level behaviour. Finally, we show how common knowledge (Kripke semantics based definition) can be obtained after observing set of examples for explicit evidence rule based systems.

Let T and S be commuting contractions on a Hilbert space H. A vector x is called a joint coboundary if it lies in the range of both I − T and I − S, and a double coboundary if it lies in the range of (I − T)(I − S). Every double coboundary is clearly a joint coboundary, and we study when the converse holds. We show that, in general, the inclusion is strict: there exist commuting unitary operators, and even commuting contractions arising from measure-preserving actions, for which some joint coboundaries fail to be double coboundaries.

On the other hand, we obtain sufficient conditions, expressed through spectral properties and the closedness of the relevant ranges, under which the two notions coincide. Applications to the joint behavior of ergodic averages and to the solvability of coupled cohomological equations are discussed.

This work examines kinetic theory models of wealth distribution in a market economy, focusing especially on how power-law tails arise. In a Boltzmann-type setting, agents trade wealth in binary exchanges that mix a conservative part with a stochastic part standing for risk and speculation. From the master equation that follows, we derive approximations of Fokker-Planck type in the regime of small exchanges and find the stationary distributions explicitly.

We prove that if the agents are divided into groups that differ in their saving propensity or their level of risk, every group converges to its own exponential or gamma-type equilibrium with a distinct characteristic scale. Wealth across the entire population is therefore a superposition of these exponentials. We show analytically that this overlap, when weighted by an appropriate distribution of scales, produces a Pareto power-law tail whose exponent is set by the statistics of the parameters. Numerical simulations of the corresponding particle system agree with the analytical predictions and display convergence to the stationary profiles.

This paper describes a novel method for abdominal multi-organ segmentation using voxel-level Siamese representation learning. It suggests that most state-of-the-art medical image segmentation procedures only evaluate geographic location, rather than the deep interaction between areas. By using Siamese representation learning, the proposed model works at the voxel level to extend the knowledge of complex physiological differences between various abdominal organ states. A number of studies were conducted, utilizing various standard abdominal organ segmentation datasets, which tested the effectiveness and validity of our method.

The findings demonstrate excellent efficiency in capturing the complex connections between abdominal tissues and sophisticated anatomical systems, leading to improved segmentation accuracy for many abdominal tissues, in contrast to previous leading approaches.

Let $X1, X2,\dots, Xn$ denote i.i.d.~centered standard normal random variables, then the law of the sample variance $Qn=\sum{i=1}^n(Xi-\bar{X})^2$ is the $\chi^2$-distribution with $n-1$ degrees of freedom. It is an open problem in classical probability to characterize all distributions with this property and in particular, whether it characterizes the normal law.

In this paper we present a solution of the free analog of this question and show that the only distributions, whose free sample variance is distributed according to a free $\chi^2$-distribution, are the semicircle law and more generally so-called \emph{odd} laws, by which we mean laws with vanishing higher order even cumulants. In the way of proof we derive an explicit formula for the free cumulants of $Q_n$ which shows that indeed the odd cumulants do not contribute and which exhibits an interesting connection to the concept of $R$-cyclicity.

Azimuthal angular decorrelation of dijet systems provides a sensitive probe of QCD radiation patterns and of parton dynamics at small Bjorken x. This paper presents a study of jet azimuthal decorrelation in deep inelastic electron–proton scattering at the proposed Future Circular Collider in electron–proton mode (FCC-ep), in which a 60 GeV electron beam collides with a 50 TeV proton beam at a centre-of-mass energy of approximately 3.5 TeV. Simulated events are generated with leading-order and next-to-leading-order matrix elements matched to parton showers, and jets are reconstructed using the anti-kT algorithm within a realistic detector acceptance.

The distribution of the azimuthal angle difference between the two leading jets is measured as a function of jet transverse momentum, photon virtuality, and rapidity separation. A clear decorrelation is observed, increasing with rapidity separation, and its magnitude is compared with predictions based on DGLAP and BFKL evolution. The results demonstrate that FCC-ep will extend the accessible kinematic range by more than an order of magnitude relative to HERA, enabling stringent tests of small-x QCD dynamics and potential sensitivity to gluon saturation effects.

Brits return Keane to number one Keane have made it a hat-trick of UK number ones with their latest offering, "Perfect Symmetry". The band scored their first number one in 2004 with "Somewhere Only We Know", followed by "Is It Any Wonder?" in 2006. "Perfect Symmetry" has now held on to the top spot for a second week, becoming the fastest-selling release of 2008, the BBC has reported. The album saw off competition from Leona Lewis, who slipped to number two with her debut, "Spirit", and Muse, who entered at three with "The Resistance".

Keane's achievement marks the first time in a year that the same artist has held the top spot for two consecutive weeks. The last artist to do so was Cascada with "Everytime We Touch" and "What Hurts the Most". Keane, who released their debut, "Hopes and Fears", in 2004, said they are "delighted" with the news. The group released "Perfect Symmetry" in October after a five-year break. Frontman Tom Chaplin recently told the BBC that the album's title summed up the album's content.

Should Universities Teach Skills or Theory? Every year, millions of students walk into university lecture halls with a question in the back of their minds: what will all this lead to? For some, the answer should be a good job. For others, it should be a better way of thinking. The debate over whether universities should teach practical job skills or theoretical knowledge touches on what higher education is really for. People who favor practical skills have a strong argument. University is expensive, and graduates often leave with significant debt. They want assurance that their degree will lead to employment.

Courses that teach coding, accounting, nursing or engineering practice can give students abilities they can use on the first day of work. Internships and project-based classes also help students understand what a profession is actually like before they commit to it. Employers, too, often complain that new graduates arrive knowing plenty of facts but little about how to apply them. On the other side, supporters of theoretical knowledge argue that specific skills expire quickly. The software a company uses today might be replaced in five years, and a student who learned only that tool could be left behind.

When bookstores dispose of damaged, misprinted, or unsold books they tear off the front cover to prevent the books being resold. The publisher doesn't want to pay to ship the books back, but also doesn't want stores to cheat them by taking the credit and then selling the book.

So they have the store remove the covers and return those and then throw away the rest of the book.," "It is cheaper to throw away an unsold paperback than it is to ship it back to the publisher. But the publisher isn't going to take the booksellers word for it, they have to tear off the front cover to make the book unsellable then send the covers back to get credit. Those books are then known as stripped books and are supposed to be destroyed.

This paper explores concept of thin games with symmetry and concurrent Hyland-Ong games. Thin games are a class of infinite games played on a graph, where players take turns to move along the edges. The paper introduces a notion of symmetry for thin games, which captures idea that game remains the same under certain transformations. Concurrent Hyland-Ong games are generalization of thin games that allow for multiple players to move simultaneously.

The paper investigates relationship between thin games with symmetry and concurrent Hyland-Ong games, and provides characterization of when thin game with symmetry can be represented as a concurrent Hyland-Ong game. The results of this study contribute to a deeper understanding of structure and properties of thin games with symmetry, and provide insights into the relationship between different classes of infinite games.

Plants don't have nervous systems or brains, but there is a growing body of research showing that they sense their surroundings, exchange information, and adjust their behavior in response to other organisms. Whether to call this "communication" in the strict sense is debated, but the evidence for chemical and electrical signaling between and within plants is strong. Airborne chemical signals The best-known examples involve volatile organic compounds (VOCs), chemicals that plants release into the air. Herbivore warnings. In the 1980s, researchers reported that willow trees and sugar maples seemed to respond to nearby trees that were being attacked by insects.

Early studies were criticized for weak controls, but later and better-designed work has supported the idea. Lima bean plants attacked by spider mites, for instance, release a blend of VOCs that attracts predatory mites that eat the pests. Neighboring bean plants exposed to those chemicals turn on their own defense genes before they are attacked. Sagebrush. Experiments by Richard Karban and colleagues showed that sagebrush clipped to mimic herbivore damage released compounds that made neighboring plants less likely to be eaten over the following season. FeSe offers an ideal platform for pinning down the electronic origin of rotational symmetry breaking in iron-based superconductors, because its nematic phase appears at around 90 K without any long-range magnetic order alongside it. We used high-resolution angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy on mechanically detwinned single crystals to follow how the electronic structure changes, resolved by momentum and orbital character, through the nematic transition.

At low temperature, the dxz/dyz splitting at the Brillouin zone corner is about 50 meV, which sets the characteristic nematic energy scale; near the zone center the splitting is far smaller, so the order parameter depends strongly on momentum. One result is especially striking: in the nematic state we see just one electron pocket, and within our experimental resolution the pocket expected at the Y point is missing.

Reaching for the Stars Without Neglecting Home Each year, governments pour billions into rockets, probes, and telescopes, even as millions of people go without clean water, medical care, or education. Critics naturally argue that this money should be spent on Earth. But setting space exploration and earthly problems against each other misreads how progress works in both. The argument against space funding carries real emotional force. One Mars mission could pay for hospitals or vaccination drives. While people are suffering today, money for faraway planets can look like a luxury that only rich countries can afford.

Yet space budgets are smaller than many people think. NASA gets under half a percent of the U.S. federal budget, a sliver of what defense or health programs receive. Even more important, space research pays for itself in practical ways. Satellites follow hurricanes, watch over crops, and measure climate change. Technology originally built for spaceflight has improved water purification, medical imaging, and solar power. Space programs also motivate students to go into science and engineering.

A barber named Elias Moreno was the first to spot it, which was fitting, since no one spends more time looking at mirrors than a barber. On a Tuesday morning he was trimming the back of Mr. Hollis's neck when he looked up and saw his reflection raising the scissors half a second behind him. It was slight, just a lag, like a video call on a poor connection. Elias paused. His reflection paused a beat later. He blinked. In time, his reflection blinked too. "Is something wrong?" asked Mr. Hollis.

"No," said Elias, and went on cutting, and did not look up again for the rest of the day. By Thursday it was everywhere. People filmed themselves waving at their bathroom mirrors and posted the clips with bewildered captions. The delay kept growing. Half a second turned into a full second, then two. Scientists appeared on the news with careful expressions and used phrases like "optical anomaly" and "under investigation," which everyone took to mean they had no idea. None of them knew, and nobody on this side ever had, that mirrors did not reflect anything. They were windows.

We describe a formulation for studying the quench dynamics of integrable systems generalizing an approach by Yudson. We study the evolution of the Lieb-Liniger model, a gas of interacting bosons moving on the continuous infinite line and interacting via a short range potential. The formalism allows us to quench the system from any initial state. We find that for any value of repulsive coupling independently of the initial state the system asymptotes towards a strongly repulsive gas, while for any value of attractive coupling, the system forms a maximal bound state that dominates at longer times.

The talent scheduling problem is a simplified version of the real-world film shooting problem, which aims to determine a shooting sequence so as to minimize the total cost of the actors involved. The cruelty of it was that the sky stayed bright. On the morning of the Blanking, everyone with eyes knew the sun was still overhead, warming their faces, and not one of them could see it. At 10:14 a.m. Eastern, it struck everywhere on Earth at once. Planes kept flying only because an autopilot needs no eyes; cars had no such luck. By noon the hospitals were swamped, and the doctors inside them were as helpless as the patients. Marguerite Oyelaran had been blind since the age of six.

That morning she was making coffee in her Baltimore apartment, and she noticed nothing wrong until her neighbor began to scream. Following the sound, she went next door and found him crawling across his kitchen floor, knocking things over. She knelt down and took his hand. "Mr. Kowalski," she said. "Stop moving. Breathe. You're going to learn this." It was the first lesson, and millions more were coming. Inside a week, the world's roughly forty million blind people were the only part of humanity still able to function. They could cross streets by listening to the traffic.

Predicting protein properties such as solvent accessibility and secondary structure from its primary amino acid sequence is an important task in bioinformatics. We study the cohomological structure of commuting tuples of contractions on Hilbert space, focusing on the joint and double coboundary operators associated with such tuples. For a commuting pair of contractions, we characterize when a given operator can be written as a joint coboundary or as a double coboundary, in terms of the convergence of suitable series built from the iterates of the contractions. We show that these conditions can be expressed through norm estimates on ergodic averages, and we establish a connection with the existence of solutions to the associated coboundary equations.

Counterexamples demonstrate that, unlike the single-operator case, the natural analogues of the classical coboundary criteria may fail without additional assumptions. We also discuss consequences for ergodic theorems and for the behavior of commuting measure-preserving transformations.

A fractal is a geometric object that displays self-similarity, meaning that its parts resemble the whole at different scales of magnification, and whose complexity is measured by a fractional, or non-integer, dimension. Although fractals began as abstract constructions in pure mathematics, Benoit Mandelbrot argued in The Fractal Geometry of Nature (1982) that they describe many natural forms more faithfully than the smooth figures of Euclidean geometry. Clouds, as he observed, are not spheres, and mountains are not cones. Coastlines offer the classic illustration.

Because a coastline is irregular at every scale, its measured length increases as the measuring unit becomes smaller, a result known as the coastline paradox. Fractal dimension provides a more meaningful description than length alone; the west coast of Great Britain, for example, has a dimension of approximately 1.25. Living systems frequently adopt fractal architectures because such structures maximize surface area or coverage within a limited volume. The branching of the human airways and blood vessels, like that of trees and root systems, enables the efficient exchange and distribution of gases, fluids, and nutrients.

Whether universities should focus on practical job skills or theoretical knowledge is a question with no simple answer. Supporters of practical training point out that students pay high tuition and expect to be employable. Courses in coding, accounting or clinical practice give graduates abilities employers want immediately, and internships let students test their interest in a career before committing to it. For many families, a degree that leads to a stable job is the whole purpose of going. Defenders of theory respond that specific skills go out of date quickly.

A programming language learned this year may be obsolete in ten, while an understanding of mathematics, statistics, or the principles of economics stays useful. Theoretical study also trains people to question assumptions, weigh evidence and write clearly, which are valuable in any field. In my view, universities should aim for a balance with theory as the foundation. Students need deep understanding to adapt as industries change, but they also need chances to apply it, through projects, placements and partnerships with employers.

There was supposed to be a delay in the beam parallel to the Earth 's rotation . The idea was that since the beam parallel to the Earth 's rotation is travelling with the Earth , it is going to have to fight against this rotation , and will therefore be delayed in recombining . Deaths of Putin Critics Fuel Suspicion as Kremlin Denies Role MOSCOW — Over the past two decades, a troubling pattern has drawn international attention: critics of Russian President Vladimir Putin and his government have been killed, jailed or forced into exile. For many observers, activists and relatives of the victims, it is no coincidence. The Kremlin, however, has consistently and firmly rejected any suggestion that it targets political opponents. Opposition figures, human rights groups and Western governments have pointed to a long list of cases. Journalists who investigated corruption or the conflict in Chechnya have been shot or poisoned.

Politicians who challenged the government have been gunned down, imprisoned or driven abroad. Supporters of those critics say the frequency of such incidents cannot be explained by chance, and they argue that a climate of impunity encourages violence against those who speak out. "People who criticize the authorities in Russia understand the risks," said one activist, who spoke on condition of anonymity out of concern for personal safety. "Every time it happens, the message is the same." Kremlin officials reject that claim.

In this work, we take a closer look on conditional generative models by creating a disentanglement structure. We re-evaluate the ability of current conditional systems to disentangle and study the impact of explicit conditioning (feature concatenation at layers) and the absence thereof (using the global latent code). We find models with explicit conditioning disentangle significantly more than their unconditional predecessors, however fail to find meaningful disentangled features. In particular, we say that the disentanglement problem in conditional models can be resolved by regularizing the feature extractors to minimize collapse.

We propose a novel regularization approach and experimentally show that it leads to meaningful outcomes for both generative models and conditional GANs. To show that these solutions work, we use the CelebA-Hair dataset and develop them quantitatively using an extensive assessment method based on the commonly used conditional GAN evaluation metric Frechet Inception Distance (FID).

Epanechnikov Mean Shift is a simple yet empirically very effective algorithm for clustering. It localizes the centroids of data clusters via estimating modes of the probability distribution that generates the data points, using the 'optimal' Epanechnikov kernel density estimator. However, since the procedure involves non-smooth kernel density functions, the convergence behavior of Epanechnikov mean shift lacks theoretical support as of this writing - most of the existing analyses are based on smooth functions and thus cannot be applied to Epanechnikov Mean Shift.

In this work, we first show that the original Epanechnikov Mean Shift may indeed terminate at a non-critical point, due to the non-smoothness nature. Based on our analysis, we propose a simple remedy to fix it. The modified Epanechnikov Mean Shift is guaranteed to terminate at a local maximum of the estimated density, which corresponds to a cluster centroid, within a finite number of iterations. We also propose a way to avoid running the Mean Shift iterates from every data point, while maintaining good clustering accuracies under non-overlapping spherical Gaussian mixture models.

A fractal is a mathematical object that exhibits detail at every scale of magnification, usually through self-similarity, and whose fractal dimension need not be an integer. Although ideal fractals such as the Koch curve exist only in theory, many physical systems approximate fractal geometry over a finite range of scales, which makes the concept a valuable descriptive tool. Natural structures provide the clearest examples. Coastlines, river networks, mountain ranges, and clouds display irregular, repeating patterns whose measured length or area depends on the scale of measurement, a property Benoit Mandelbrot famously analyzed.

Biological systems show similar organization: the branching of bronchial passages and blood vessels packs enormous surface area into limited volume, supporting efficient exchange and transport. Fractal geometry also emerges from physical processes. Diffusion-limited aggregation produces branching clusters resembling lightning and electrodeposition patterns, while chaotic dynamical systems often evolve on strange attractors with fractal structure. Scale-invariant behavior near critical points in phase transitions is likewise closely related to fractal scaling. These ideas have practical value. Fractal analysis informs antenna design, image compression, medical diagnostics, and the modeling of porous materials and terrain. The analogy has limits, however.

In this paper, we consider the problem of quantifying controllability and observability of a nonlinear discrete time dynamical system. We introduce the Koopman operator as a canonical representation of the system and apply a lifting technique to compute gramians in the space of full-state observables. We illustrate the properties of these gramians and identify several relationships with canonical results on local controllability and observability. Once defined, we show that these gramians can be balanced through a change of coordinates on the observables space, which in turn allows for direct application of balanced truncation.
Throughout the paper, we highlight the aspects of our approach with an example nonlinear system.

The Hunchback of Notre Dame is a novel by Victor Hugo, published in 0923. The novel tells the story of Quasimodo, the deformed bell ringer of Notre-Dame Cathedral, and his unrequited love for the beautiful gypsy dancer, Esmeralda. A direct English translation of the French title would be "The Hunchback" or "The Hunchback of Our Lady". The story begins on the Feast of Fools in Paris in 1482. Quasimodo, the deformed bell ringer of Notre Dame, is being led through the streets as part of the festival.

He is treated harshly by the crowd, who pelts him with stones and ridicule him. He is then rescued by Claude Frollo, the Archdeacon of Notre Dame. Frollo takes Quasimodo back to the cathedral and raises him as his own. Quasimodo grows to love Notre Dame and its people, but he is always an outcast because of his deformity. One day, he meets Esmeralda, a beautiful gypsy dancer. He is immediately smitten with her and falls in love. However, Frollo is also attracted to Esmeralda and becomes obsessed with her. When Esmeralda rejects Frollo's advances, he lashes out at her.

This year the smells and sounds were the same, but the moment I stepped into the foyer, every conversation stopped for exactly one heartbeat too long. "Danny!" She hugged me with the stiff tenderness of someone holding a bomb. I had told exactly one person. My mother. The Bank of France has published a report on the economy, in which it finds that the principal source of growth is constituted by the expenditure of the consumers. They constitute over two-thirds of the growth of the national economy. They also give that foreign commerce and domestic investment are of equal importance in the maintenance of growth. The results of this investigation correspond to the last calculations of the Bank of France, which have shown that the growth of consumption and of industrial investment constituted, in the second quarter, the principal source of the growth of the national economy.

This is expected to continue for the next few months; on the other hand, the domestic investment and the foreign commerce are expected to decline in the near future. Convolutional neural networks owe much of their success on images to the regular grid structure and translation symmetry of the plane, neither of which exists on curved surfaces. A common workaround maps a surface to a planar domain and applies a standard CNN, but existing surface-to-image representations either introduce large area distortion or require several images to cover the whole shape. We propose a new representation for sphere-type surfaces based on general covering maps.

Rather than relying on a toric cover with a fixed set of cone points, our construction lets a flat torus wrap around the surface several times, so that every region appears with low distortion somewhere in a single image. Because this image is seamless and periodic, convolution with circular padding is well defined, and off-the-shelf architectures apply with minimal modification. Predictions from the multiple copies of each surface point are then aggregated back onto the mesh. Experiments on shape segmentation and classification benchmarks show that the method matches or exceeds competing approaches while remaining simple and efficient.

Empirical studies of income and wealth consistently find an exponential, or Boltzmann–Gibbs, distribution for most of the population and a Pareto power-law tail for the wealthiest few percent. Kinetic exchange models, in which agents trade wealth through random binary interactions that conserve the total, naturally reproduce the exponential bulk. Producing a power-law tail, however, generally requires additional assumptions. In this paper we show that a power law can arise from the superposition of exponential distributions. We consider a heterogeneous population in which each agent has a saving propensity drawn from a prescribed distribution.

Within the framework of kinetic theory, we derive the Boltzmann-type equation that governs the evolution of wealth. We show that in the long-time limit, each subpopulation defined by a given saving propensity relaxes to a distribution with an approximately exponential tail, and the scale of that tail depends on the propensity. When these partial distributions are aggregated, their overlap produces a Pareto tail whose exponent is set by the behavior of the saving-propensity distribution near its upper limit. Monte Carlo simulations of the underlying agent-based dynamics support the analytical results.

We traced the traffic to a test box in the corner, a machine we had nicknamed Zombie because it had been "decommissioned" three times and kept coming back. Someone had left it plugged in, and it was happily hammering our staging environment with requests from a script nobody remembered writing. "Kill it," Marcus said. "I can't SSH in," I said. "It's not on the network." "It's clearly on the network." "The dashboard says it's on the network. The dashboard also thinks it's 1970." Priya was already on her knees under the desk. Working from Home: Benefits and Drawbacks In recent years, working from home has become common in many countries. Improvements in technology and changes brought by the pandemic have allowed millions of people to do their jobs without going to an office. This shift has clear advantages, but it also brings real disadvantages. The most obvious benefit is flexibility. Employees save the time and money they would otherwise spend commuting, and many use those hours to sleep, exercise, or be with family. Remote workers can often arrange their schedules around personal needs, which can improve both happiness and productivity.

Employers also gain, since they may spend less on office space and can hire talented people from anywhere rather than only from nearby. In addition, fewer commuters means less traffic and lower carbon emissions, which is good for the environment. However, working from home is not without problems. One major issue is isolation. Without daily contact with coworkers, people can feel lonely and disconnected, and casual conversations that spark ideas or build friendships tend to disappear. Another difficulty is separating work from private life.

We extend the theory of Cellular Automata to arbitrary, time-varying graphs. In other words we formalize, and prove theorems about, the intuitive idea of a labelled graph which evolves in time - but under the natural constraint that information can only ever be transmitted at a bounded speed, with respect to the distance given by the graph. The notion of translation-invariance is also generalized. The definition we provide for these "causal graph dynamics" is simple and axiomatic. The theorems we provide also show that it is robust.

For instance, causal graph dynamics are stable under composition and under restriction to radius one. In the finite case some fundamental facts of Cellular Automata theory carry through: causal graph dynamics admit a characterization as continuous functions, and they are stable under inversion. The provided examples suggest a wide range of applications of this mathematical object, from complex systems science to theoretical physics. KEYWORDS: Dynamical networks, Boolean networks, Generative networks automata, Cayley cellular automata, Graph Automata, Graph rewriting automata, Parallel graph transformations, Amalgamated graph transformations, Time-varying graphs, Regge calculus, Local, No-signalling.

The desert sand swirled as the winds began to shift. It was afternoon and the sun shone high overhead, burning the dry, cracked desert floor. Somewhere a cicada shrilled its cry into the air. The gunman in black, still on his knees from when the standing gunman had found him, stared into the dirty water of the spring. He'd die here. "I found you." The voice of the standing gunman was soft, the words leaving his lips with purpose and a cleanliness to them. Tucker was twenty-nine now. It'd taken him nine years to find the man before him.

"You got me, kid," replied the crouching man, still staring at the small amount of water that remained in the spring. "You got me dead to rights." He licked his lips. "I always knew you would, too, if'n I was tellin' the truth, boy. You're a good kid, your father would be proud." Tucker pressed the barrel of his gun against the back of his captor's head. "Don't you mention my Pa, Clive, you don't deserve to speak of him." Clive and four others had waited outside of a saloon till John, Tucker's father, had come out near dark.

A standard chessboard has 64 squares if you count only the individual light and dark squares. If you count every square that can be traced on the board, including larger squares made up of smaller ones, the answer is 204. Counting squares of every size In addition to the 1 × 1 squares, the 8 × 8 grid contains 2 × 2 squares, 3 × 3 squares, and so on, up to the entire board, which is itself one 8 × 8 square. The key is to count how many positions each size can occupy.
Take a 2 × 2 square. Its top-left corner can sit in any of the first 7 columns and any of the first 7 rows, so there are 7 × 7 = 49 of them.

Let me begin by saying that I was never desperate to start a family. I believe that a childless life can be just as fulfilling as a life with children, only in a different way. So to me, it's a decision that needs to be weighed up. From the evidence I can gather, there is a high probability the climate change will start to have major impacts on humanity by 2060. I am not really worried about a higher rate of natural disasters; we have natural disasters today and we know how to deal with them.

What I am worried about are secondary social and economic effects. Wars over dwindling resources. Civil unrest. Mass migration. Financial crises. Failed states. Mitigation is not likely to happen, or at least not until it's too late. Some individual humans have foresight, but as a group we have about as much foresight as an ant colony. North-south asymmetry of sunspot activity resulted in an asynchronous reversal of the Sun's polar fields in the current cycle. The asymmetry is also observed in the formation of polar coronal holes. A stable coronal hole was first formed at the South Pole, despite the later polar-field reversal there. The aim of this study is to understand processes making this situation possible.

Synoptic magnetic maps from the Global Oscillation Network Group and corresponding coronal-hole maps from the Extreme ultraviolet Imaging Telescope aboard the Solar and Heliospheric Observatory and the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly aboard the Solar Dynamics Observatory are analyzed here to study a causal relationship between the decay of activity complexes, evolution of large-scale magnetic fields, and formation of coronal holes. Ensembles of coronal holes associated with decaying active regions and activity complexes are presented. These ensembles take part in global rearrangements of the Sun's open magnetic flux.

This paper presents а theoretical analysis of broadband and energy-concentrating terahertz (THz) coherent perfect absorbers based on а self-complementary metasurface. The proposed approach utilizes periodic arrays of metal nanoparticles arranged in а specific pattern, which allows it to achieve complete absorption across various wavelengths within the THz frequency band. Τо demonstrate this concept, we conducted numerical simulations using FDTD methodology with results showing that our design achieves over 90% broadband coherent perfect absorption for waves between 2.5 and 6 THz.

Furthermore, we illustrate an energy-concentration mechanism enabling enhanced interaction between incident radiation and embedded antennas through polarization-dependent scattering, making the proposed structure а promising candidate for future applications such as THz sensing and imaging systems. Overall, our work provides new insights into the potential functionality of metamaterials in THz technology, opening up exciting avenues for further research.

A barber named Elias Moreno noticed it first. He was cutting Mr. Hollis's neck on Tuesday morning and saw his reflection holding the scissors half a second late. Just a lag, like a bad video call. He stopped. His reflection stopped after him. By Thursday it was everywhere—people filming themselves in mirrors, posting confused clips. Delay kept growing. Half a second became a full second, two seconds. Scientists on TV with careful faces said "optical anomaly," which everyone knew meant they had no idea. What nobody knew was mirrors weren't reflecting anything. They were windows.

Another Earth on the other side, perfect copy, left and right swapped. For all of history the two worlds moved in perfect lockstep. Every gesture matched. Until something over there slipped. Maybe an atom decayed wrong. Maybe a butterfly flapped the wrong way. The two worlds started drifting and it kept accelerating. Two weeks in, people weren't just seeing delays. They were seeing different things. A woman in Ohio watched her reflection brush its teeth while she stood still. A teenager in Seoul saw his reflection walk out of frame, leaving an empty bedroom behind the glass.

"Four out of five dentists recommend" is a marketing claim, and what it actually means hinges on how the survey behind it was carried out. Companies do poll dentists at times, but these samples tend to be small and the questions are often worded vaguely. Dentists might simply be asked if they would recommend a product, or they might be permitted to list more than one brand, so numerous brands can each say they are endorsed by most dentists. As a result, the number does not necessarily mean that 80 percent of dentists favor that particular toothpaste over every other.
Shoppers should check the sample size, the precise wording of the question, and whether there is independent endorsement, such as a seal from a recognized dental association.

Mining frequent tree patterns has many applications in different areas such as XML data, bioinformatics and World Wide Web. The crucial step in frequent pattern mining is frequency counting, which involves a matching operator to find occurrences (instances) of a tree pattern in a given collection of trees. A widely used matching operator for tree-structured data is subtree homeomorphism , where an edge in the tree pattern is mapped onto an ancestor-descendant relationship in the given tree. Tree patterns that are frequent under subtree homeomorphism are usually called embedded patterns .

In this paper, we present an efficient algorithm for subtree homeomorphism with application to frequent pattern mining. We propose a compact data-structure, called occ , which stores only information about the rightmost paths of occurrences and hence can encode and represent several occurrences of a tree pattern. We then define efficient join operations on the occ data-structure, which help us count occurrences of tree patterns according to occurrences of their proper subtrees. Based on the proposed subtree homeomorphism method, we develop an effective pattern mining algorithm, called TPMiner. We evaluate the efficiency of TPMiner on several real-world and synthetic datasets.

This paper proposes novel approach for optimizing spectral efficiency in flexi-grid long-haul optical systems. Flexi-grid systems are becoming increasingly popular due to their ability to accommodate diverse transmission formats and flexible grid spacings, but they also present challenges in terms of spectral efficiency. The proposed approach utilizes combination of advanced modulation formats, adaptive optics, and nonlinear optimization techniques to maximize the spectral efficiency of system. The proposed approach is evaluated using a detailed simulation framework that takes into account impact of various impairments, such as noise, dispersion, and nonlinearities, on system performance.

The results show that proposed approach significantly improves the spectral efficiency of the system compared to traditional fixed-grid systems and existing flexi-grid systems. In addition, the proposed approach is found to be robust against variations in transmission distance, launch power, and number of channels, making it suitable for a wide range of long-haul optical communication applications. The paper also provides a comprehensive analysis of trade-offs between spectral efficiency, transmission distance, and signal quality, which is essential for designing practical long-haul optical systems.

Gunmen Kill at Least 23 at Tunisia's Bardo Museum TUNIS, Tunisia — At least 23 people were killed Wednesday when gunmen stormed the Bardo National Museum in the Tunisian capital, targeting one of the country's best-known cultural landmarks and the tourism industry on which its economy depends. Most of the dead were foreign visitors, several of whom had come ashore earlier that day from cruise ships docked in Tunis. Security forces ended a standoff inside the museum by killing two of the attackers, and dozens of people were treated for injuries.

The Bardo, which houses one of the world's great collections of Roman mosaics, sits next to the national parliament. The attack has shaken a country often described as the one success story of the Arab Spring. Since the 2011 revolution that ousted President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali, Tunisia has adopted a new constitution and held free elections. Yet it has also become one of the largest sources of foreign fighters for extremist groups in Syria and Iraq, with an estimated 3,000 Tunisians believed to have joined them.

Curiosity is a car-sized Mars rover designed to explore the Gale crater on Mars as part of NASA's Mars Science Laboratory (MSL) mission. Curiosity was launched from Cape Canaveral (CCAFS) on November 26, 2011, at 15:02:00 UTC and landed on Aeolis Palus inside Gale crater on Mars on August 6, 2012, 05:17:57 UTC. The Bradbury Landing site was less than 2.4 km (1.5 mi) from the center of the rover's touchdown target after a 560 million km (350 million mi) journey.

Mission goals include an investigation of the Martian climate and geology, assessment of whether the selected field site inside Gale has ever offered environmental conditions favorable for microbial life (including investigation of the role of water), and planetary habitability studies in preparation for human exploration.

The IceCube Neutrino Observatory is a multi-component detector at the South Pole which detects high-energy particles emerging from astrophysical events. These particles provide us with insights into the fundamental properties and behaviour of their sources. Besides its principal usage and merits in neutrino astronomy, using IceCube in conjunction with its surface array, IceTop, also makes it a unique three-dimensional cosmic-ray detector. This distinctive feature helps facilitate detailed cosmic-ray analysis in the transition region from galactic to extragalactic sources. We will present the progress made on multiple fronts to establish a framework for mass-estimation of primary cosmic rays.

The first technique relies on a likelihood-based analysis of the surface signal distribution and improves upon the standard reconstruction technique. The second uses advanced methods in graph neural networks to use the full in-ice shower footprint, in addition to global shower-footprint features from IceTop. A comparison between the two methods for composition analysis as well as a possible extension of the analysis techniques for sub-PeV cosmic-ray air-showers will also be discussed.

The symmetry requirement and the origin of magnetic orders coexisting with superconductivity have been strongly debated issues of iron-based superconductors (FeSCs). Observation of C$4$-symmetric antiferromagnetism in violation of the inter-band nesting condition of spin-density waves in superconducting ground state will require significant change in our understanding of the mechanism of FeSC.

The superconducting material Sr$2$VO$3$FeAs, a bulk version of monolayer FeSC in contact with a perovskite layer with its magnetism (T$N$ ~ 50 K) and superconductivity (T$c$ ~ 37 K) coexisting at parent state, has no reported structural orthorhombic distortion and thus makes a perfect system to look for theoretically expected C$4$ magnetisms. Based on variable temperature spin-polarized scanning tunneling microscopy (SPSTM) with newly discovered imaging mechanism that removes the static surface reconstruction (SR) pattern by fluctuating it rapidly with spin-polarized tunneling current, we could visualize underlying C$4$ symmetric (2$\times$2) magnetic domains and its phase domain walls.

Deaths and Imprisonments of Putin Critics Prompt Suspicion; Kremlin Denies Allegations MOSCOW — For many opponents of Vladimir Putin, criticizing the Russian president has carried a heavy cost. Across the past twenty years, a series of critics, journalists and political rivals have been shot, poisoned or jailed, a pattern that human rights groups and Western governments say chance cannot explain. The Kremlin flatly rejects that reading, maintaining that it had no part in the deaths and that those in prison were convicted of real crimes in Russian courts.

The latest case to attract international attention was the killing of Boris Nemtsov, a former deputy prime minister and outspoken opposition leader who was shot dead on a bridge within sight of the Kremlin walls. At the time he died, Nemtsov had been working on a report about Russian military involvement in eastern Ukraine. Several men from Chechnya were arrested and later convicted, but Nemtsov's allies say those who ordered the killing have never been named. His death came after a long run of similar cases.

It happened on a Tuesday, which seemed unfair. Gods shouldn't have to remember things on Tuesdays. I was standing in the grocery store checkout—holding eggs and a laundry detergent coupon—when it hit me. Not like a thought. Like remembering your own phone number. Oh. Right. I'm God. The stars, the platypus, that weird orange on the fruit stand across the aisle. All me. I'd just stepped away for a while. The woman in front of me was arguing with the cashier about a banana. Not the price, just the banana.

And something opened up in my chest so huge my knees buckled. I knew exactly how many hairs she had. I knew she cried in her car that morning. I dropped the eggs. Twelve of them, all over the floor. "Sir? You okay?" "I made you," I said. It came out gentler than I meant, way scarier than I wanted. She stepped back. The banana woman stared. The kid at the next register was reaching for his phone. Ten seconds. Ten seconds before a video. Here's what I understood in those ten seconds. Being God isn't like being a king.

Finally, space budgets are relatively small compared to other government spending, so cutting them would not end poverty. In conclusion, space exploration and solving earthly problems are not opposites. By investing in space, governments also invest in a better future on Earth.

Firefighters were called to the scene in Craigton Place, Winchburgh, at about 01:30 after a wheelie bin was set on fire. Thirty homes in the area were evacuated, with 38 residents temporarily housed at a local community centre. They were eventually allowed to return home at about 06:30.

'Young children' Police are treating the blaze as wilful fire-raising and appealed for information about the West Lothian incident. They are keen to trace anyone who may have seen someone in the area just before the bin was set alight. Det Con Adrian Wallis said: "This was a serious incident which could have had devastating consequences. "It also resulted in the evacuation of over 30 people, including young children and elderly residents. This caused much alarm and upset to those who had to leave their homes in the middle of the night.

As a general trend in industrial robotics, an increasing number of safety functions are being developed or re-engineered to be handled in software rather than by physical hardware such as safety relays or interlock circuits. This trend reinforces the importance of supplementing traditional, input-based testing and quality procedures which are widely used in industry today, with formal verification and model-checking methods. To this end, this paper focuses on a representative safety-critical system in an ABB industrial paint robot, namely the High-Voltage electrostatic Control system (HVC).

The practical convergence of the high-voltage produced by the HVC, essential for safe operation, is formally verified using a novel and general co-verification framework where hardware and software models are related via platform mappings. This approach enables the pragmatic combination of highly diverse and specialised tools. The paper's main contribution includes details on how hardware abstraction and verification results can be transferred between tools in order to verify system-level safety properties. It is noteworthy that the HVC application considered in this paper has a rather generic form of a feedback controller.

This paper examines the properties of space-time by utilizing the non-compressible solutions of Navier-Stokes equations. The Navier-Stokes equations are set of partial differential equations that describe the motion of fluid substances. By analyzing these equations, it is possible to derive the properties of space-time and gain insights into its fundamental nature. The study presents mathematical framework for analyzing the equations and identifies key properties of space-time, such as its smoothness and conservation laws.
The paper also discusses the implications of these findings in context of general relativity and quantum mechanics, providing deeper insights into nature of space-time and its role in universe.

The US dollar has weakened against a basket of major currencies, as investors become increasingly cautious in the lead up to the new year. The dollar index, which measures the greenback's performance against six other prominent currencies, fell by 0.3% on Thursday to 96.54. This marks a third consecutive day of declines for the currency, with investors seeming to favored safer-haven assets such as gold and the Japanese yen. The downturn in the dollar's fortunes comes amidst growing concerns about the global economic outlook, particularly in light of the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic and geopolitical tensions.

Traders are also anxiously awaiting the outcome of next week's meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, where they will discuss the fate of their nations' long-standing trade dispute. Despite these uncertainties, some analysts believe that the dollar's slide may be temporary, citing strong underlying economic fundamentals in the United States. "While there are certainly risks on the horizon, the US economy is still performing well, with low unemployment and steady growth," said Jane Foley, a senior currency strategist at Rabobank London.

A double-helix electrode configuration is combined with $^{10}$B powder coating technique to build large-area (9 in $\times$ 36 in) neutron detectors. The neutron detection efficiency for each of four prototypes is comparable to a single 2-bar $^3$He drift tube of the same length (36 in). One unit has been operational continuously for 18 months and the change of efficiency is less than 1%. An analytic model for pulse heigh spectra is described and the predicted mean film thickness agrees with experiment to within 30%. Further detector optimization is possible through film texture, power size, moderator box and gas.
The estimated production cost per unit is less than 3k US\$ and the technology is thus suitable for deployment in large numbers.

Every year, millions of graduates leave university with a degree in hand and the same question on their minds: what can I actually do now? That question is at the center of a long-running debate over whether higher education should focus on practical job skills or on theoretical knowledge. Those who favor practical training make a strong economic case. University is expensive, and many students take on serious debt to attend, so they reasonably expect their studies to lead to stable jobs.

Employers often complain that graduates arrive without basic workplace abilities such as writing a clear report, working in a team, or using common software. A curriculum built around internships, projects, and industry tools would help close this gap and smooth the move from classroom to career. On the other hand, defenders of theory argue that a university is not just a training center. Technology and job markets change quickly, and a skill that is valuable today may be useless in ten years. Theory teaches students to reason, question assumptions, and understand why things work.

A total solar eclipse occurred over the northeastern Australian coast early in the morning of November 14 local time. Clueless about this spectacular astronomical event? No worries, we've got you covered. We're here to explain what causes this remarkable act of nature, what skygazers see and how those outside of Australia can join in the experience. What exactly is a total solar eclipse? A solar eclipse happens when the moon, as it orbits Earth, passes directly in front of the sun, obscuring its rays and casting a shadow on Earth's surface.

Sometimes referred to as a "happy accident of nature," a total solar eclipse occurs when the moon is perfectly aligned with both the sun and Earth, so it appears from our perspective that the sun is completely blocked. When is this happening and who can see it? The total solar eclipse became visible in the far north of Australia about an hour after sunrise local time on November 14 (afternoon of November 13 in the United States and evening of November 13 in Europe).

"Whale Wars" TV conservationist Paul Watson quit his conservation society Tuesday because of a recent federal court injunction against him and his group's anti-whaling activities. Last month, the Japanese research foundation Institute of Cetacean Research and the Japanese firm Kyodo Senpaku Kaisha Ltd. secured a U.S. District Court injunction against Watson and his Sea Shepherd Conservation Society, according to the institute's website. The injunction prohibits Watson and his group from coming within 500 yards of the plaintiffs on the open sea, according to a copy of the court document on the institute's website.
Watson has become renowned for his attempts to disrupt Japanese whalers on the open water through Animal Planet's "Whale Wars" TV show.
